item.title: A single antimatter particle was held in a trap for months
item.description: Some of the equipment used to trap a single positron Gabrielse group/Northwestern University In a lab in Illinois, physicists captured and tamed a tiny particle of antimatter in a trap with invisible walls. By studying how the positron behaved, the researchers may soon have a chance to break our best mathematical model of physical reality. The positron is the antimatter counterpart of the electron, which means the two particles have the same mass but the opposite electric charge. Unlike electrons, however, positrons are rare and typically exist for a tiny fraction of a second because the moment one meets one of the super-abundant electrons in our universe, the pair annihilate. This makes positrons difficult to study. Gerald Gabrielse at Northwestern University in Illinois and his colleagues have now found a way to trap a positron and keep it around for months on end. By analysing data collected while the positron was trapped, they plan to precisely measure the antiparticle’s properties and consequently investigate one of the biggest problems with the standard model of particle physics . Advertisement Read more LHC finds intriguing new clues about our universe’s antimatter mystery The researchers obtained the positron from a radioactive isotope of sodium that emits one whenever it decays. Such positrons are very fast and hard to control, so they placed the sodium into a special refrigerator to lower its temperature and energy, and slow down the antiparticles. They slowed them further by directing the positrons through a tungsten crystal. While some positrons were annihilated as they travelled through the crystal, some came through unscathed. They were then directed into a refrigerated chamber that was empty of all other particles. Here, electronic components generated electromagnetic fields that confined a single incoming positron, serving as invisible walls that trapped the particle. The researchers then pushed the positron into its lowest possible energy state, which Gabrielse says allowed them to keep the otherwise elusive antiparticle trapped for months. They could also push it into the next lowest energy state with controlled bursts of microwaves. Subscriber-only newsletter Sign up to Editor’s Highlights Sign up to newsletter “It’s a real kick to stand in my lab and watch a positron making transitions – ‘quantum jumps’ we call them – between its lowest energy states. How much more fundamental, how much neater can it get?” he says. “Trapping an antiparticle is extremely difficult,” says Stefan Ulmer at Japanese scientific institute RIKEN, particularly since any stray particle, burst of light or tiny vibration could disturb it and the trap had to be kept just tenths of a degree above the coldest temperature possible. The payoff for trapping and controlling the positron despite these experimental challenges could be remarkable. “This has the potential to become one of the most precise measurements of a fundamental constant in physics,” says Ulme
item.dc:creator: Karmela Padavic-Callaghan
item.content:encoded: Some of the equipment used to trap a single positron Gabrielse group/Northwestern University In a lab in Illinois, physicists captured and tamed a tiny particle of antimatter in a trap with invisible walls. By studying how the positron behaved, the researchers may soon have a chance to break our best mathematical model of physical reality. The positron is the antimatter counterpart of the electron, which means the two particles have the same mass but the opposite electric charge. Unlike electrons, however, positrons are rare and typically exist for a tiny fraction of a second because the moment one meets one of the super-abundant electrons in our universe, the pair annihilate. This makes positrons difficult to study. Gerald Gabrielse at Northwestern University in Illinois and his colleagues have now found a way to trap a positron and keep it around for months on end. By analysing data collected while the positron was trapped, they plan to precisely measure the antiparticle’s properties and consequently investigate one of the biggest problems with the standard model of particle physics . Advertisement Read more LHC finds intriguing new clues about our universe’s antimatter mystery The researchers obtained the positron from a radioactive isotope of sodium that emits one whenever it decays. Such positrons are very fast and hard to control, so they placed the sodium into a special refrigerator to lower its temperature and energy, and slow down the antiparticles. They slowed them further by directing the positrons through a tungsten crystal. While some positrons were annihilated as they travelled through the crystal, some came through unscathed. They were then directed into a refrigerated chamber that was empty of all other particles. Here, electronic components generated electromagnetic fields that confined a single incoming positron, serving as invisible walls that trapped the particle. The researchers then pushed the positron into its lowest possible energy state, which Gabrielse says allowed them to keep the otherwise elusive antiparticle trapped for months. They could also push it into the next lowest energy state with controlled bursts of microwaves. Subscriber-only newsletter Sign up to Editor’s Highlights Sign up to newsletter “It’s a real kick to stand in my lab and watch a positron making transitions – ‘quantum jumps’ we call them – between its lowest energy states. How much more fundamental, how much neater can it get?” he says. “Trapping an antiparticle is extremely difficult,” says Stefan Ulmer at Japanese scientific institute RIKEN, particularly since any stray particle, burst of light or tiny vibration could disturb it and the trap had to be kept just tenths of a degree above the coldest temperature possible. The payoff for trapping and controlling the positron despite these experimental challenges could be remarkable. “This has the potential to become one of the most precise measurements of a fundamental constant in physics,” says Ulmer. Six ways we could finally find new physics beyond the standard model Leading physicists explain how they think we will discover the new particles or forces that would complete one of science’s greatest unfinished masterpieces Specifically, Gabrielse and his colleagues want to measure the positron’s magnetic moment, which is a number that quantifies its response to magnetic fields. The researchers have previously made the most precise ever measurement of the electron’s magnetic moment, and comparing this figure with the one for the antiparticle would enable them to compare the properties of matter and antimatter with unprecedented precision. The standard model predicts they should have identical magnetic moments, but this prediction underscores a notable shortcoming of this theory. The problem is that if matter and antimatter are so alike, then they should have been created in equal amounts and fully annihilated as the universe began, leaving nothing. “The standard model seems to be inconsistent, or at least significantly incomplete, with basic features of the universe, like why we have a universe at all,” says Gabrielse. Uncovering a difference between the electron and positron could hint at some currently unknown mechanism that resulted in our matter-filled universe. If all goes according to plan, the researchers aim to have data that will shed light on this within the year. Journal Reference: Physical Review Letters DOI: 10.1103/gbkc-6nlj

The conversational Gemini in navigation is available today for US drivers, with "rollout happening globally too," according to Google (we've asked for specific regional availability details). item.title: Jensen Huang sends in the robot ducks to sell Nvidia's AI-everywhere vision
item.description: Cute robots stole the show at Nvidia's GTC keynote in Berlin, where Jensen Huang pitched a future powered by AI agents – and, naturally, plenty of his company's hardware. The Nvidia chief remained his usual ebullient self despite environmental protesters interrupting his presentation at Berlin's tent-shaped Tempodrom. "Why don't you clean up your act?" they demanded, holding up banners that partially obscured the presentation screen behind Huang. "All important issues, but let me get through my keynote," he joked, adding: "I'll talk to you guys later," as security swiftly removed them. Huang was discussing Vera Rubin systems before unveiling DSX POD, a reference design for factory-built, containerized AI infrastructure . DSX POD combines seven liquid-cooled Vera Rubin compute racks using Nvidia's Spectrum-X networking. Partners will cable, integrate, and test the systems in modular containers before delivery, with availability expected in early 2027. Nvidia claims deployment could shrink from six months to as little as 14 days at a prepared site. That excludes the not insignificant matter of getting power, connectivity, and other site infrastructure ready first. He was keen to add that Vera Rubin systems are designed for closed-loop liquid cooling with coolant temperatures up to 45°C, while outdoor dry coolers release heat into the air without needing to evaporate water. "At 2 gigawatts, DSX can save 54 million litres of water a day," Huang claimed, perhaps thinking of those environmental protesters. Yet much of the leather-jacketed leader's attention was focused on physical AI: robots, autonomous vehicles, and other machinery Nvidia hopes to supply with its hardware and software. The Microducks from Pollen Robotics are small, two-legged robots with cameras for faces. Huang interacted with them on stage, getting them to lie down and roll over by voice command, and the little robots all beeped back at him in response. The robo ducks demonstrated a workflow in which AI was trained in the cloud, evaluated on an Nvidia RTX Spark PC, then deployed on the robots. Huang also unveiled Agile ONE SN, a humanoid robot reference platform from German robotics startup Agile Robots, based on Nvidia's Isaac GR00T technology and a Jetson Thor compute module. Scheduled for early 2027, the platform is intended to give robotics researchers and developers a ready-made system for developing and testing capabilities. "This is going to be the next major industry, the next great industry," Huang claimed. Beyond robots, Nvidia is pushing its AI hardware and software into cars and telecoms networks. Huang boasted that Nvidia's Hyperion car system is being adopted by more vendors, saying: "We turned this into an industry standard, and now it's being designed into one car fleet after another." Europe's telecoms operators are also deploying Nvidia-powered computing in their networks to deliver advanced services using AI-RAN, according to Huang. "After working on this for near

Nvidia claims deployment could shrink from six months to as little as 14 days at a prepared site. That excludes the not insignificant matter of getting power, connectivity, and other site infrastructure ready first. He was keen to add that Vera Rubin systems are designed for closed-loop liquid cooling with coolant temperatures up to 45°C, while outdoor dry coolers release heat into the air without needing to evaporate water. "At 2 gigawatts, DSX can save 54 million litres of water a day," Huang claimed, perhaps thinking of those environmental protesters. Yet much of the leather-jacketed leader's attention was focused on physical AI: robots, autonomous vehicles, and other machinery Nvidia hopes to supply with its hardware and software. The Microducks from Pollen Robotics are small, two-legged robots with cameras for faces. Huang interacted with them on stage, getting them to lie down and roll over by voice command, and the little robots all beeped back at him in response. The robo ducks demonstrated a workflow in which AI was trained in the cloud, evaluated on an Nvidia RTX Spark PC, then deployed on the robots. Huang also unveiled Agile ONE SN, a humanoid robot reference platform from German robotics startup Agile Robots, based on Nvidia's Isaac GR00T technology and a Jetson Thor compute module. Scheduled for early 2027, the platform is intended to give robotics researchers and developers a ready-made system for developing and testing capabilities. "This is going to be the next major industry, the next great industry," Huang claimed. Beyond robots, Nvidia is pushing its AI hardware and software into cars and telecoms networks. Huang boasted that Nvidia's Hyperion car system is being adopted by more vendors, saying: "We turned this into an industry standard, and now it's being designed into one car fleet after another." Europe's telecoms operators are also deploying Nvidia-powered computing in their networks to deliver advanced services using AI-RAN, according to Huang. "After working on this for nearly eight years, Nvidia made the first commercial phone call on the T-Mobile network with Nokia, and so now CUDA makes phone calls," he said. Far from slowing down the progression of AI, it seems Nvidia is determined to push its technology into every corner of the world. "Everyone will become an AI company," Huang claimed. He also took care to praise Europe and its technology efforts while he was in Berlin. "As expected, Jensen positioned Nvidia as a strong supporter of – and enabler for – Europe's sovereign tech ambitions. Nvidia has invested almost $10 billion into Europe in the past year, including 14 investments into European startups during Jensen's current trip," said Forrester principal analyst Paul Miller. But Miller pointed out that Nvidia itself is not European. "Anything with critical ongoing dependencies on Nvidia (or any other non-European firm) is unlikely to meet the purest definitions of European tech sovereignty," he added. Huang closed with a CGI video of robots performing a Eurovision-style song recapping his keynote. Yes, it was as bad as you imagine. ®

item.title: The Entire Internet Is Officially In Crisis Mode Today
item.description: Don't be surprised if your favorite website is completely down on Wednesday. A massive security risk has just been discovered, and it impacts nearly every popular website on the internet. That includes websites like Wikipedia, Slack, Spotify, and even Pornhub just to name a few. WordPress at large is at risk, and that platform is estimated to power nearly a fourth of the internet .

item.title: Otti to flag off Aba, Umuahia court complexes in November
item.description: By Steve Oko UMUAHIA — Abia State Governor, Dr Alex Otti, has announced plans to flag off the construction of ultra-modern court complexes in Aba and Umuahia in November. Each complex, according to the governor, will have an auditorium with a seating capacity of 1,000. Otti also announced plans to commission 15 additional court halls in phases, with 10 scheduled for commissioning after the current Legal Year programme and five before the end of the year. The remaining court hall is expected to be commissioned early next year. The governor made the announcements on Tuesday during the 2026/2027 Legal Year Thanksgiving Service held at the Queen Elizabeth Chapel, Federal Medical Centre, Umuahia. He said his administration was also working towards digitising processes across the executive, legislature and judiciary to improve efficiency and access to government services. Speaking on the theme of the Legal Year, “The Bar, the Bench and the Administration of Justice: Strengthening the Courts that Bind,” Otti stressed the need for cooperation among the three arms of government while preserving their constitutional independence. “The judiciary is a very important arm of government. There is no way the Executive or the legislature can work without the judiciary. But then, the lines are also very clear. And one thing you can be sure of with us is that we will always maintain those lines,” he said. The governor congratulated members of the Bar and Bench on the commencement of the new Legal Year and commended their commitment to due process and the rule of law. The Chief Judge of Abia State, Justice Lilian Abai, commended the working relationship between the executive and the judiciary, describing it as “a cord worth strengthening.” She disclosed that the state government had installed solar power systems at the High Courts in Umuahia and Aba. Abai also said Otti signed three laws on October 19: the Abia State Administration of Criminal Justice Law, 2026; the Abia State Restorative Justice Law No. 8 of 2026; and the Abia State Criminal Law No. 7 of 2026. She urged lawyers to protect the integrity of the judiciary and maintain a constructive relationship with the Bench. Earlier, the Anglican Bishop of Umuahia Diocese, Rt. Rev. Geoffrey Ibeabuchi, urged legal practitioners to discharge their duties with sincerity and accountability. He encouraged them to emulate King Solomon’s quest for wisdom and understanding, noting that members of the public relied on the legal profession for protection against oppression. The event was attended by dignitaries from the judiciary, government and other sectors. The post Otti to flag off Aba, Umuahia court complexes in November appeared first on Vanguard News .

item.title: 23-year-old Iranian woman sentenced to death over social media post
item.description: Iranian authorities sentenced a 23-year-old student to death for blasphemy in social media posts, rights groups said, as the judiciary’s use of capital punishment on political charges mounts. Najmeh Amini was arrested in February in the northeastern city of Mashhad and sentenced to death in September on charges of insulting the Prophet Mohammed, rights groups including the US-based Center for Human Rights in Iran (CHRI), Human Rights Activists News Agency (HRANA) and the Norway-based Iran Human Rights (IHR) said in separate statements. Iran has already hanged 34 men on charges related to the January 2026 protests. But at least eight women, as well as Amini, are facing execution on political and security charges, according to rights groups. “I am an innocent girl. A young person with so many hopes and dreams. I have a mother and father who are waiting for me, a family who spend every night afraid of losing me until morning comes,” Amini said in an audio message from prison in September that was shared by the rights groups. “Remember my name. Perhaps I won’t be able to speak anymore. But as long as I am alive, I have one hope: that before the rope becomes the end of my life, I will see a free and liberated Iran.” The use of blasphemy charges, a capital crime in the Islamic republic, had been relatively rare in recent years. Bahar Ghandehari, director of advocacy at the CHRI, told AFP the “authorities may… be using this rare and severe verdict to make an example of her (Amini) and discourage similar acts as popular discontent continues to increase”. “Her case reflects the broader escalation of arbitrary arrests, politically motivated prosecutions, and death sentences following the bloody crackdown on protesters,” she added. – ‘Life at stake’ – “Amini’s life is at stake, and the international community must act urgently to stop her execution,” Ghandehari said. The verdict is not final and still subject to appeal. Details of her trial remain sparse, but according to reports in the regional daily Khorosan, Amini’s lawyer argued her posts were not intentional while Amini said she had been under the influence of hallucinogenic mushrooms she had consumed with friends. The precise nature of the posts was unclear. She was sentenced to death on charges of “sabb al-nabi”, the capital crime of insulting the Prophet Mohammed, according to the CHRI. In a separate case, the accounting student was also sentenced to 12 and a half years in prison for acting against national security. HRANA said Amini has been tracked by Iran’s FATA cyber police after the protests, which peaked in mid-January. Mass rallies in Mashhad and other big cities were suppressed in a crackdown rights groups say left thousands dead. “Amini was held in prolonged isolation, subjected to physical beatings during arrest, and entirely denied access to a lawyer of her choice,” it said. item.title: Samsung’s 5K monitor has good gaming chops and a great price
item.description: There are quite a few 5K monitors out there. Many of them are designed to appeal to Mac users who are looking for cheaper Studio Display alternatives without giving up the pixel-dense 218ppi screen. However, if you’re interested in hearing about one with gaming chops, Samsung’s 27-inch Odyssey G80HF seems like one of the best monitors out there to satisfy your niche, but respectable desires. Currently, you can grab this model for $599.99 at Amazon and B&H Photo , which beats its best price by $100. Samsung 27-inch Odyssey G8 5K monitor Where to Buy: $949.99 $599.99 at Amazon $949.99 $599.9 at B&H Photo The G80HF supports two display modes with its Fast IPS panel: 5K at up to 180Hz refresh rate, or 1440p with up to a 360Hz refresh rate. Samsung touts Nvidia G-Sync compatibility as well as AMD FreeSync Premium to ensure the monitor’s refresh rate remains in lockstep with your GPU’s frame rate output. The monitor features a DisplayPort 2.1 port (just one, and Samsung doesn’t advertise its bandwidth), two HDMI 2.1 ports, and a USB hub for charging or connecting two USB-A 3.2 Gen 1 accessories. As a gamer, one of my favorite features here is the one-millisecond response time. That’s a very common spec among gaming monitors — even in ones that cost hundreds less — but it’s a bit of a rare spec in a 5K monitor at this price. I tested KTC’s sub-$500 model last year , and gaming on it was a pretty atrocious experience despite having what it claimed to be gaming-ready capabilities. For $200 more ($799.99), LG’s 27-inch UltraGear evo 5K Mini LED monitor delivers slightly better specs. It has more dimming zones for a more accurate picture, it can get brighter, and it supports USB-C video input with 90W power delivery output to charge your device as you use it. Its dual mode refresh rates aren’t as high as Samsung’s (165Hz / 330Hz), but I don’t really see that as much of a downside. Other great deals happening now For those who haven’t yet placed a preorder for Grand Theft Auto VI , which comes out in less than a month, you can do so while saving $10 on a gaming gift card at Best Buy. The retailer is letting customers build a bundle of select games and gift cards. You can, for example, add GTA VI and a gift card will be $10 off its advertised price at checkout. It’s a small, but welcome way to save a little cash. The bundle includes other current and upcoming blockbusters, like Gears of War: E-Day , Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 , and more. The excellent remake of Demon’s Souls by the shuttered PlayStation studio , Bluepoint Games, is down to just $13.49 in digital format on the PlayStation Store. What’s more, it’s for the digital deluxe edition (originally $89.99), which includes in-game cosmetics, a consumable that grants you a bunch of souls for in-game upgrades, and the soundtrack. The sale lasts through November 4th on the West Coast, or until 2:59AM ET on November 5th on the East Coast. The remake doesn’t mess with the formula of FromSoftware’s PS3 cul

It’s a small, but welcome way to save a little cash. The bundle includes other current and upcoming blockbusters, like Gears of War: E-Day , Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 , and more. The excellent remake of Demon’s Souls by the shuttered PlayStation studio , Bluepoint Games, is down to just $13.49 in digital format on the PlayStation Store. What’s more, it’s for the digital deluxe edition (originally $89.99), which includes in-game cosmetics, a consumable that grants you a bunch of souls for in-game upgrades, and the soundtrack. The sale lasts through November 4th on the West Coast, or until 2:59AM ET on November 5th on the East Coast. The remake doesn’t mess with the formula of FromSoftware’s PS3 cult classic (it has stages instead of being an open-world like its spiritual successor, Dark Souls ), but gives it some brilliant visuals and fast loading times. It’s definitely worth a try if you’re into other Soulslike games that reward (and test) your patience. Read our review of the game . If you need a multi-port wall charger to quickly charge a bunch of USB-C devices, Ugreen’s Nexode Pro is down to $59.99 at Amazon and Ugreen , a $30 discount off the usual cost. The price was $10 lower during June’s Prime Day, but this is still a nice value. Despite the charger advertising 160W charging passthrough, its USB-C ports labeled C1 and C2 each top out at 140W when just one device is plugged into the charger. The power of each port (four USB-C, one USB-A) varies depending on how many gadgets are plugged in, up to 160W total. The charger has folding prongs and a display that can rotate depending on how it’s plugged in.

item.title: “I Never Really Thought of Insects as Beautiful Creatures” – Dara Ojo on Becoming a Macro Photographer
item.description: Nigerian Macro Photographer, Dara Ojo. In 2020, during the COVID-19 pandemic, Dara Ojo was stuck at home in China, like everyone else in the world. He had recently picked up photography, and that allowed him to explore and pay close attention to his immediate surroundings. One day, he started paying closer attention to the tiny creatures around him and was amazed by what he was seeing. There were colours, patterns, behaviours and details that he had never noticed before. It felt like discovering an entirely different world that had been right in front of me all along. Dara self-taught himself macro photography, and the seemingly small curiosity during the pandemic has grown into a journey of documenting biodiversity across Nigeria, Canada, Costa Rica, Mexico, Ecuador and beyond. His work has travelled globally and has been featured in major international publications. Dara has photographed over 40 types of spiders, 50 species of moths, 30 species of butterflies, more than 20 dragonflies, and at least 70 damselflies. There are many photographers in Nigeria, but seeing that macro photography is not often explored by Nigerians, we sat down for a brief conversation with Dara, where he shared what inspired his form of photography, what documenting biodiversity in different environments has taught him about nature and his forthcoming first photography book, Tiny Titans: The Silent Keepers of Our Ecosystem. Leafhopper infected by Metarhizium Fungus. Photo by Dara Ojo. Hey Dara, how are you feeling? I feel good. I feel blessed. Thank you for having me. What do you think inspired or attracted you to macro photography? Growing up in Nigeria, I never really thought of insects as something beautiful or worth photographing. Like many people, I saw them as creatures you either avoided or tried to get rid of. But once I started looking at them through my camera, my perspective completely changed. What fascinated me most wasn’t just how they looked, but how they lived. I started asking questions. Why does this spider behave this way? How does that tiny insect survive? What role does it play in nature? The more I discovered, the more curious I became. Six years later, that curiosity has taken me from photographing tiny creatures around my neighbourhood in China to exploring rainforests and other ecosystems across different continents. And the interesting thing is that I still experience that same excitement whenever I discover something new. I don’t think that feeling will ever go away. Bumblebee by macro photographer, Dara Ojo. The excitement. How can you describe it? When taking a shot, what do you feel that you hope people also feel when they encounter the photo? Wonder. That’s probably the best word to describe it. Sometimes I’m photographing a creature, and I genuinely cannot believe what I’m looking at. It might be the incredible colours of a jumping spider, the delicate patterns on a moth’s wings, or an insect doing something I’ve never witnessed before. T
item.dc:creator: BellaNaija Features
item.content:encoded: Nigerian Macro Photographer, Dara Ojo. In 2020, during the COVID-19 pandemic, Dara Ojo was stuck at home in China, like everyone else in the world. He had recently picked up photography, and that allowed him to explore and pay close attention to his immediate surroundings. One day, he started paying closer attention to the tiny creatures around him and was amazed by what he was seeing. There were colours, patterns, behaviours and details that he had never noticed before. It felt like discovering an entirely different world that had been right in front of me all along. Dara self-taught himself macro photography, and the seemingly small curiosity during the pandemic has grown into a journey of documenting biodiversity across Nigeria, Canada, Costa Rica, Mexico, Ecuador and beyond. His work has travelled globally and has been featured in major international publications. Dara has photographed over 40 types of spiders, 50 species of moths, 30 species of butterflies, more than 20 dragonflies, and at least 70 damselflies. There are many photographers in Nigeria, but seeing that macro photography is not often explored by Nigerians, we sat down for a brief conversation with Dara, where he shared what inspired his form of photography, what documenting biodiversity in different environments has taught him about nature and his forthcoming first photography book, Tiny Titans: The Silent Keepers of Our Ecosystem. Leafhopper infected by Metarhizium Fungus. Photo by Dara Ojo. Hey Dara, how are you feeling? I feel good. I feel blessed. Thank you for having me. What do you think inspired or attracted you to macro photography? Growing up in Nigeria, I never really thought of insects as something beautiful or worth photographing. Like many people, I saw them as creatures you either avoided or tried to get rid of. But once I started looking at them through my camera, my perspective completely changed. What fascinated me most wasn’t just how they looked, but how they lived. I started asking questions. Why does this spider behave this way? How does that tiny insect survive? What role does it play in nature? The more I discovered, the more curious I became. Six years later, that curiosity has taken me from photographing tiny creatures around my neighbourhood in China to exploring rainforests and other ecosystems across different continents. And the interesting thing is that I still experience that same excitement whenever I discover something new. I don’t think that feeling will ever go away. Bumblebee by macro photographer, Dara Ojo. The excitement. How can you describe it? When taking a shot, what do you feel that you hope people also feel when they encounter the photo? Wonder. That’s probably the best word to describe it. Sometimes I’m photographing a creature, and I genuinely cannot believe what I’m looking at. It might be the incredible colours of a jumping spider, the delicate patterns on a moth’s wings, or an insect doing something I’ve never witnessed before. There have been moments when I’ve found myself laughing out of excitement because nature has surprised me again. That’s the feeling I want people to experience when they see my photographs. I know some people might initially feel uncomfortable looking at a spider or another creature they’re afraid of, and that’s perfectly understandable. But if they can look at that photograph for a few more seconds and begin to notice something fascinating rather than frightening, then I feel I’ve accomplished something. I’m not necessarily trying to make everyone love insects or spiders. I just want people to become curious enough to see them differently. Because sometimes, curiosity is all it takes to change how we treat the natural world. Silk Worm Moth by Nigerian macro photographer, Dara Ojo As someone who has photographed in different parts of the world, how has documenting biodiversity in different environments shaped your perspective on nature? One of the biggest things I’ve learned is that extraordinary biodiversity isn’t limited to the places we traditionally associate with wildlife photography. I’ve photographed in China, Costa Rica, Mexico, Ecuador, Canada and Nigeria, and every environment has taught me something different. In the rainforests of Costa Rica and Ecuador, I’ve encountered creatures with some of the most remarkable adaptations I’ve ever seen. In Canada, I’ve spent countless hours photographing tiny wildlife in places people walk past every day. Even a small garden can be home to an incredible diversity of species. But returning to photograph in Nigeria was particularly meaningful to me. Treehopper by Nigerian macro photographer, Dara Ojo. What do you think people might be surprised to learn about Nigeria’s insect life and biodiversity? I think many Nigerians would be surprised by just how much biodiversity exists in our own country. Nigeria has an extraordinary range of habitats, from tropical rainforests in the south to savannas in the north, supporting an incredible variety of life. When people think about African wildlife, the conversation often centres on lions, elephants and other large animals. But there’s an entire world of smaller creatures that rarely receive the same attention. During my time photographing in Nigeria, I encountered some fascinating species, including the praying mantis that eventually became the cover of my book. And that’s something I find particularly special. After travelling across different continents and photographing so many remarkable creatures, the photograph chosen to represent my first book came from Nigeria. It reminds me that we don’t always have to travel halfway around the world to discover something extraordinary. Sometimes, we simply need to pay closer attention to what’s around us. Mantis, by Nigerian macro photographer Dara Ojo. Let’s talk about the book Yes! Tiny Titans: The Silent Keepers of Our Ecosystem . My first photography book. Tell us about it and what you hope people take away from the book? This book means a great deal to me because it represents six years of curiosity, exploration and learning. It brings together around 120 of my photographs from different parts of the world, alongside stories about the creatures I’ve encountered and the important roles they play in nature. I wanted to create something that people could enjoy visually, but that would also encourage them to think differently about creatures they might normally overlook. These tiny animals are doing some of the most important work on our planet. They pollinate plants, recycle nutrients, help control populations of other organisms and provide food for countless species. Without them, the ecosystems we depend on would look very different. Yet many are misunderstood, feared or simply ignored. What makes the book particularly meaningful to me is that it also tells a personal story. It follows my journey through different countries, including Nigeria, where I grew up, and Canada, where I now live. I’m also incredibly honoured that Dr John Acorn , a respected Canadian entomologist and science communicator, wrote the foreword. I hope someone picks up the book because they find the photographs interesting, but finishes it with a greater appreciation for the natural world, so that the next time they encounter a spider in their house or an unfamiliar insect in their garden, instead of immediately reaching for something to kill it, they’ll stop for a moment and take a closer look. _ Dara Ojo’s Tiny Titans: The Silent Keepers of Our Ecosystem will be published on November 10, 2026, and will be available internationally. It will have public book launches in Edmonton on November 25 and Toronto on December 2, with additional events being explored for New York in March 2027 and Vancouver in April 2027. You can pre-order the book here . The post “I Never Really Thought of Insects as Beautiful Creatures” – Dara Ojo on Becoming a Macro Photographer appear

item.title: UTME: Only 108 of 39,000 underage candidates scale FG’s admission hurdles
item.description: By Joseph Erunke, Abuja Only 108 out of about 39,000 underage candidates who sat the 2026 Unified Tertiary Matriculation Examination (UTME) have survived the Federal Government’s rigorous screening for possible admission into tertiary institutions, underscoring the high academic and maturity standards imposed on exceptionally young applicants. The candidates emerged after a stringent selection process that required applicants to demonstrate outstanding academic performance and psychological, emotional and intellectual readiness for university education. Minister of Education Dr Tunji Alausa disclosed this on Wednesday in Abuja while receiving the two highest-scoring candidates and six best-performing underage candidates in the 2026 UTME, presented by the Registrar of the Joint Admissions and Matriculation Board, JAMB, Prof. Segun Aina. Alausa said the outcome followed a multi-stage screening exercise designed to ensure that admission opportunities for exceptionally gifted children would not come at the expense of their preparedness for the demands of higher education. According to him, 2,244,149 candidates registered for the 2026 UTME, while 2,174,396 eventually sat the examination. Of these, approximately 39,000 were below the prescribed minimum admission age of 16 years. The minister explained that candidates seeking exemption from the age requirement had to meet a series of demanding conditions, beginning with a minimum UTME score of 320 out of 400, representing 80 per cent. They were also required to score at least 80 per cent in their post-UTME examinations, attain the stipulated 80 per cent threshold in the assessment of their O-level results and pass a screening exercise to establish their psychological, emotional and intellectual readiness for university education. Alausa disclosed that only 391 underage candidates scored at least 320 in the UTME, with further assessments reducing the number eligible for possible admission to just 108. item.content:encoded: By Joseph Erunke, Abuja Only 108 out of about 39,000 underage candidates who sat the 2026 Unified Tertiary Matriculation Examination (UTME) have survived the Federal Government’s rigorous screening for possible admission into tertiary institutions, underscoring the high academic and maturity standards imposed on exceptionally young applicants. The candidates emerged after a stringent selection process that required applicants to demonstrate outstanding academic performance and psychological, emotional and intellectual readiness for university education. Minister of Education Dr Tunji Alausa disclosed this on Wednesday in Abuja while receiving the two highest-scoring candidates and six best-performing underage candidates in the 2026 UTME, presented by the Registrar of the Joint Admissions and Matriculation Board, JAMB, Prof. Segun Aina. Alausa said the outcome followed a multi-stage screening exercise designed to ensure that admission opportunities for exceptionally gifted children would not come at the expense of their preparedness for the demands of higher education. According to him, 2,244,149 candidates registered for the 2026 UTME, while 2,174,396 eventually sat the examination. Of these, approximately 39,000 were below the prescribed minimum admission age of 16 years. The minister explained that candidates seeking exemption from the age requirement had to meet a series of demanding conditions, beginning with a minimum UTME score of 320 out of 400, representing 80 per cent. They were also required to score at least 80 per cent in their post-UTME examinations, attain the stipulated 80 per cent threshold in the assessment of their O-level results and pass a screening exercise to establish their psychological, emotional and intellectual readiness for university education. Alausa disclosed that only 391 underage candidates scored at least 320 in the UTME, with further assessments reducing the number eligible for possible admission to just 108. He described the successful candidates as exceptionally gifted, noting that they represented approximately 0.005 per cent of the candidates who sat the examination. “You are the geniuses in our society,” the minister told the students, stressing that the government had a responsibility to identify exceptional talents and nurture them into innovators capable of developing solutions to Nigeria’s challenges and those of the wider world. The minister said the minimum admission age of 16 was not intended to frustrate academically gifted children or deny them opportunities to advance, but to ensure that those admitted at a younger age possessed the maturity required to cope with university life. He said the screening exercise had yielded encouraging feedback, particularly regarding the candidates’ confidence, intellectual ability and responses to questions designed to assess their preparedness for higher education. According to him, exceptional academic performance alone cannot be the sole basis for admitting children into tertiary institutions, as university education also demands emotional stability and the capacity to navigate its social and intellectual challenges. Alausa urged the successful candidates to see their academic abilities as a responsibility to society, rather than merely an opportunity to secure early admission and personal advancement. “You are the ones that will change Nigeria and change the world with your innovations,” he said. The minister linked the recognition of exceptional young talents to the country’s broader development prospects, arguing that Nigeria’s youthful population represented a major resource that must be properly educated and harnessed. He put Nigeria’s population at an estimated 220 million, with an average age of 18.5 years, adding that about 70 per cent of the population was below 30. Alausa said the Federal Government’s education reforms were designed to expand opportunities for young Nigerians and strengthen the country’s capacity to turn their potential into innovations and solutions that could improve lives. He congratulated the candidates on behalf of President Bola Tinubu and the Federal Ministry of Education, expressing confidence that their abilities could translate into breakthroughs capable of benefiting millions of people. The eight recognised candidates, including the two highest scorers in the 2026 UTME, received plaques and certificates from the minister. Owoeye Daniella Jesudunsin emerged as the highest-scoring candidate with 372 marks, while Enwere Kingsley Ikenna followed with 370. item.title: FG urges self-care to contain Ebola
item.description: The Federal Government has urged Nigerians to practise self-care, including regular hand hygiene and appropriate disinfection, to support efforts to contain Ebola virus disease following confirmation of an imported case in Abuja. The Minister of State for Health and Social Welfare, Dr Iziaq Salako, made the call on Tuesday in Abuja at the inaugural National Self-Care Conference 2026, themed “Self-Care Puts Your Health in Your Hands: Test. Track. Thrive.” Salako emphasised the importance of individual responsibility in preventing and controlling infectious diseases, urging Nigerians to adopt healthy practices and cooperate with public health officials to contain Ebola. “Let me emphasise that self-care is also important in the prevention and control of infectious diseases, including Ebola viral disease, which Nigeria is currently working hard to contain, following one imported case that was reported. “I therefore use this opportunity to call on the Nigerian public to observe self-care, like hand hygiene and appropriate disinfection, and cooperate fully with public health officials to contain the reported Ebola in this case,” he said. He said self-care empowered people with the knowledge, skills and tools to take charge of their health while extending healthcare beyond hospitals and clinics into homes, workplaces and communities. According to him, self-care complemented professional healthcare rather than replacing it or absolving the government of its responsibility to provide accessible, affordable and quality health services. “As government, therefore, we will continue to promote investment in health facilities, skilled personnel, essential medicines, and functional referral systems,” he said. Salako said self-care could strengthen primary healthcare, advance universal health coverage and improve outcomes in maternal and reproductive health, non-communicable diseases and mental well-being. He explained that “Test” encouraged people to establish their health status, “Track” promoted consistent monitoring of health indicators and treatment adherence, while “Thrive” represented the goal of healthier individuals, stronger families and more resilient communities. The minister urged state governments to integrate evidence-based self-care into health policies and programmes, while calling on healthcare professionals to guide its safe use and development partners to support sustainable financing and capacity development. The Special Adviser to the President on Health, Dr Salma Anas, said self-care should be promoted alongside effective regulation, quality services and accountability to prevent unsafe practices and ensure people received appropriate support. Anas said the Federal Government remained committed to achieving universal health coverage without leaving anyone behind while maintaining the quality of healthcare services. item.content:encoded: The Federal Government has urged Nigerians to practise self-care, including regular hand hygiene and appropriate disinfection, to support efforts to contain Ebola virus disease following confirmation of an imported case in Abuja. The Minister of State for Health and Social Welfare, Dr Iziaq Salako, made the call on Tuesday in Abuja at the inaugural National Self-Care Conference 2026, themed “Self-Care Puts Your Health in Your Hands: Test. Track. Thrive.” Salako emphasised the importance of individual responsibility in preventing and controlling infectious diseases, urging Nigerians to adopt healthy practices and cooperate with public health officials to contain Ebola. “Let me emphasise that self-care is also important in the prevention and control of infectious diseases, including Ebola viral disease, which Nigeria is currently working hard to contain, following one imported case that was reported. “I therefore use this opportunity to call on the Nigerian public to observe self-care, like hand hygiene and appropriate disinfection, and cooperate fully with public health officials to contain the reported Ebola in this case,” he said. He said self-care empowered people with the knowledge, skills and tools to take charge of their health while extending healthcare beyond hospitals and clinics into homes, workplaces and communities. According to him, self-care complemented professional healthcare rather than replacing it or absolving the government of its responsibility to provide accessible, affordable and quality health services. “As government, therefore, we will continue to promote investment in health facilities, skilled personnel, essential medicines, and functional referral systems,” he said. Salako said self-care could strengthen primary healthcare, advance universal health coverage and improve outcomes in maternal and reproductive health, non-communicable diseases and mental well-being. He explained that “Test” encouraged people to establish their health status, “Track” promoted consistent monitoring of health indicators and treatment adherence, while “Thrive” represented the goal of healthier individuals, stronger families and more resilient communities. The minister urged state governments to integrate evidence-based self-care into health policies and programmes, while calling on healthcare professionals to guide its safe use and development partners to support sustainable financing and capacity development. The Special Adviser to the President on Health, Dr Salma Anas, said self-care should be promoted alongside effective regulation, quality services and accountability to prevent unsafe practices and ensure people received appropriate support. Anas said the Federal Government remained committed to achieving universal health coverage without leaving anyone behind while maintaining the quality of healthcare services. She cited contraceptive self-injection as an example of an intervention that promoted independence and autonomy in family planning. The presidential adviser cautioned against interpreting self-care as government withdrawal from its healthcare responsibilities. “You can take responsibility because you have to acknowledge you are sick and acknowledge what you can do within the comfort of your home before you even reach the health services,” she said. Anas also emphasised the importance of community participation, appropriate regulation and accountability in implementing self-care interventions. Dr Mary Brantuo, Coordinator, Strategic Health Policy and Planning at the World Health Organization (WHO), described the conference as a demonstration of Nigeria’s commitment to empowering people to take greater control of their health. She said self-care could help address gaps in access to services amid persistent challenges involving maternal and child mortality, unmet family planning needs, infectious diseases and non-communicable diseases. “Self-care is not about replacing health systems but is rather about extending the reach of health systems and empowering people with the knowledge, tools, and confidence they need to make informed decisions about their health,” Brantuo said. She identified HIV self-testing, contraceptive self-injection and self-monitoring as interventions that had demonstrated their value and acceptability in Nigerian communities. The Group Chief Executive Officer of the Society for Family Health (SFH), Dr Omokhudu Idogho, said self-care required accurate information, quality products, affordable services and access to professional care. Represented by Mr Emeka Okafor, Group Director, Population, Health and Community Systems, Donor-Funded Portfolio Directorate, Idogho said people made health decisions in their homes, pharmacies and communities. He added that people also made health decisions through their phones, making reliable information and appropriate services in those spaces essential. Idogho said SFH was using telemedicine through its Access Care initiative to bring professional advice closer to people facing distance, transport costs, time constraints and privacy concerns. He added that the organisation’s Co-Elevate initiative highlighted the need for investment and partnerships to make technology-driven self-care services sustainable and accessible to underserved populations. Idogho said data should be used to assess who accessed self-care services, who remained excluded and whether users received appropriate follow-up care. The News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) reports that self-care is the ability of individuals, families and communities to promote health, prevent disease, maintain health and cope with illness and disability, with or without support from a healthcare provider. Self-care interventions include contraceptive self-injection, HIV self-testing, human papillomavirus self-sampling, blood pressure checks and appropriate self-monitoring of health conditions. (NAN) The post FG urges self-care to contain Ebola appeared first on Vanguard News .

item.title: IAD endorses Obi, claims 25% voter base in 31 states
item.description: By John Alechenu, Abuja The Igbo Agenda Dialogue (IAD) has endorsed Peter Obi of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) for the January 16, 2027 presidential election, claiming that Igbo people constitute at least 25 per cent of voters in 31 states and the Federal Capital Territory. The National Chairman of IAD and founder of the All Progressives Grand Alliance (APGA), Chief Chekwas Okorie, announced the endorsement in Abuja on Wednesday. He described IAD as an Igbo political network linked to Igbo unions, market associations, women and youth groups in Nigeria and the diaspora. Okorie traced the history of Igbo political collaboration with other ethnic groups, saying the community had consistently supported alliances aimed at promoting national unity. He recalled that Dr Nnamdi Azikiwe led the independence struggle and that his party, the National Council of Nigeria and the Cameroons (NCNC), entered a coalition with the Northern People’s Congress (NPC), paving the way for Alhaji Tafawa Balewa to become Prime Minister in 1960. He also cited the Second Republic, when Azikiwe’s Nigerian People’s Party (NPP) allied with the National Party of Nigeria (NPN) to form a government. According to Okorie, during the transition programme of former Head of State, General Abdulsalami Abubakar, Igbo leaders met at Modotel Hotel in Enugu and invested politically in the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) after Dr Alex Ekwueme was assured of support from his northern political associates for the presidency. He said the South-East subsequently supported the PDP across elective positions but alleged that Ekwueme was denied the party’s presidential ticket at its Jos convention. Okorie said IAD assessed the leading contenders for the 2027 presidential election based on their records, empathy, fitness, probity and prudence before consulting widely and settling on Obi. “We came to the unanimous resolution that it will be in the best interest of Nigeria to elect Mr Peter Obi,” he said. He claimed Obi enjoyed support across ethnic and religious lines and was the most globally visible contender in the presidential race. Okorie said Nigerians had long been governed by ageing political leaders and argued that the 2027 election offered an opportunity to elect a compassionate and prudent leader, despite what he described as intimidation. On the demographic strength of the Igbo electorate, he said: “Igbo people constitute a minimum of 25% of the voting population in each of the 31 states in Nigeria and the Federal Capital Territory or the second largest population to the indigenous population of these states while constituting over 99% of the voting population in the five states in the South East.” He also announced that Obi would run with Senator Rabiu Musa Kwankwaso, a former governor of Kano State, as his running mate. Okorie urged other Igbo politicians to focus their campaigns on issues affecting Nigerians. Awolowo was appointed Minister without Portfolio by the then Premier of the Eastern Region, Dr M.I. Okpara, while her husband, Chief Obafemi Awolowo, was imprisoned in Calabar. item.title: JAMB moves to ease admission anxiety, warns against identity fraud
item.description: By Joseph Erunke, Abuja The Joint Admissions and Matriculation Board (JAMB) has introduced service improvements aimed at reducing admission-related anxiety, improving access to candidates’ accounts and ensuring a fairer admission process, while warning against identity fraud. The Registrar of JAMB, Professor Segun Aina, disclosed this on Wednesday during an interaction with Unified Tertiary Matriculation Examination (UTME) candidates at the board’s Abuja Zonal Office. He said the reforms were designed to rebuild public confidence, minimise avoidable difficulties and make the admission process more transparent. However, while promising greater flexibility for candidates seeking to correct legitimate errors in their personal information, Aina warned that anyone attempting to manipulate their identity or exploit the system would face the full weight of the law. The registrar said the board’s policy adjustments were guided by the need to build trust and reduce the difficulties candidates experience during registration and admission. “All the policy optimisation that we are doing is centred around two things: building trust and reducing trauma,” he said during the engagement, organised as part of JAMB’s 2026 Customer Week. He explained that the board was not discarding its existing operational framework but strengthening it through targeted changes to make its services more responsive to candidates’ needs. One of the major improvements, according to him, is the provision of more detailed information on candidates’ admission status, allowing applicants to better understand the progress of their applications. Previously, candidates checking their status could encounter messages such as “not admitted” or “admission in progress” without sufficient information to explain their position. Aina said the improved system would provide more details about the progress of admission applications, helping candidates avoid unnecessary uncertainty. “Building trust is necessary. That is why now you can see the progress with your admission status. Instead of just seeing ‘not admitted’ or ‘admission in progress’ and just waiting and being nervous and being traumatised, we now have a situation where you can see the details,” he said. He described the adjustment as an important step towards easing the pressure on candidates seeking admission into universities, polytechnics and other tertiary institutions. The Registrar of JAMB, Professor Segun Aina, disclosed this on Wednesday during an interaction with Unified Tertiary Matriculation Examination (UTME) candidates at the board’s Abuja Zonal Office. He said the reforms were designed to rebuild public confidence, minimise avoidable difficulties and make the admission process more transparent. However, while promising greater flexibility for candidates seeking to correct legitimate errors in their personal information, Aina warned that anyone attempting to manipulate their identity or exploit the system would face the full weight of the law. The registrar said the board’s policy adjustments were guided by the need to build trust and reduce the difficulties candidates experience during registration and admission. “All the policy optimisation that we are doing is centred around two things: building trust and reducing trauma,” he said during the engagement, organised as part of JAMB’s 2026 Customer Week. He explained that the board was not discarding its existing operational framework but strengthening it through targeted changes to make its services more responsive to candidates’ needs. One of the major improvements, according to him, is the provision of more detailed information on candidates’ admission status, allowing applicants to better understand the progress of their applications. Previously, candidates checking their status could encounter messages such as “not admitted” or “admission in progress” without sufficient information to explain their position. Aina said the improved system would provide more details about the progress of admission applications, helping candidates avoid unnecessary uncertainty. “Building trust is necessary. That is why now you can see the progress with your admission status. Instead of just seeing ‘not admitted’ or ‘admission in progress’ and just waiting and being nervous and being traumatised, we now have a situation where you can see the details,” he said. He described the adjustment as an important step towards easing the pressure on candidates seeking admission into universities, polytechnics and other tertiary institutions. JAMB eases correction of personal details Aina also disclosed that the board had deployed technology to make it easier for candidates to update their telephone numbers and email addresses, particularly when they lose access to the contact details used during registration. He said such changes had previously presented difficulties because the information served as unique identifiers within the board’s system. The new approach, he explained, was intended to help candidates regain access to their accounts and update their details without unnecessary hardship, while preserving the security of the admission process. On changes to names and other personal information, the registrar said JAMB had strengthened its collaboration with the National Identity Management Commission (NIMC) to facilitate the alignment of candidates’ records across both institutions. He commended NIMC for its cooperation and prompt response in resolving discrepancies in personal information. According to him, JAMB had relied on NIMC data during registration but imposed restrictions on changing personal details because of the risk of identity manipulation after candidates had entered the admission system. He said improvements in technology and institutional collaboration had created room for legitimate corrections under appropriate safeguards. Aina, however, cautioned that the changes should not be exploited to falsify identities or circumvent admission rules. “If you would like to change your entire name, we will keep track of you. And if you are trying to take advantage of the system, please get ready. You will be feeling the full weight of the law in due course,” he warned. Aina pledges to build on past reforms The registrar also rejected suggestions that the changes represented a wholesale rebranding of JAMB, describing his administration’s approach as a continuation of reforms introduced by previous leaderships. He particularly acknowledged the contributions of his immediate predecessor, Professor Ishaq Oloyede, to sanitising the system and expanding the use of technology in the board’s operations. “I inherited a fantastic institution. Credit to my predecessors, particularly my immediate past predecessor, Professor Ishaq Oloyede, who did a lot to sanitise the system even further and to adopt technology even further,” he said. Aina said his administration would build on those achievements by improving service delivery, strengthening accountability and sustaining public confidence in the examination and admission system. ‘UTME is a means to an end’ Beyond customer service improvements, the registrar restated what he described as the board’s central responsibility: coordinating a credible admission process rather than merely conducting examinations. He said the harmonised examination timetable, although potentially leaving JAMB with a shorter preparation period, was important to the wider education system because it helped ensure that results were released in time for institutions to conduct their admission exercises. According to him, the UTME should be viewed as a means of determining candidates’ eligibility, while the ultimate objective is to ensure that qualified applicants secure admission into appropriate programmes. “Don’t forget, we are popular for the exams, but the exam is not our only mandate. Our core, the exam is a means to an end. Our core is the admissions exercise itself,” he said. Aina maintained that candidates should not need personal connections or access to influential individuals to secure admission. He said JAMB had a responsibility to moderate interactions between candidates and tertiary institutions and ensure that qualified applicants received fair consideration under established admission requirements. “The people we serve don’t need to know anybody to get admission. It is our job to stand and moderate the interaction between these candidates and the institutions, and make sure they get their rightful places in the universities,” he said. JAMB considers critical thinking assessment In another development, Aina disclosed that the board had inaugurated a committee to examine whether critical thinking and life skills could be incorporated into its examinations. He stressed that the proposal remained under consideration and that no final decision had been taken on its adoption. The committee, headed by Professor Nwogu, a psychometrician, is expected to examine whether assessing abilities beyond conventional academic subjects could provide a more comprehensive picture of candidates’ competencies and suitability for their chosen courses. Aina explained that candidates were already required to meet the relevant O’level requirements before taking the UTME, but said the board was exploring whether additional assessment methods could help identify applicants with strong reasoning, problem-solving and decision-making abilities. He argued that academic knowledge alone might not fully capture the competencies required in professional practice, where individuals must apply knowledge to practical situations and make sound decisions. Using medicine as an example, he said healthcare professionals needed more than technical knowledge, including the ability to assess situations, make responsible decisions and understand the consequences of their actions. He said the proposed assessment would require rigorous investigation to determine whether critical thinking and life skills could be measured reliably and whether their inclusion would improve educational

item.title: Football Daily | Champions League drama galore – so why do we feel hollow?
item.description: Sign up now! Sign up now! Sign up now? Sign up now! Now then, which one of you hipsters decided to put Porto 0-1 PSV on? Oh dear. This was another night of Bigger Cup at its Bigliest self, comebacks everywhere, 40 goals in nine games, six of those in a best-v-best clash as Paris Saint-Germain rallied late against Barcelona. Even in defeat, Lamine Yamal found space to decorate the room with a ludicrous toe-poke equaliser, and there was a wholesome tale in Italy as Scott McTominay scored twice for Napoli in their 4-3 win against Bodø/Glimt. These were his first strikes since returning from heart surgery, taking his tally at the club to 29 goals in 86 appearances. No wonder Erik ten Hag was peeved with his bosses at Manchester United for shipping the midfielder off to Naples. One has to admire the courage of Erik ten Hag, speaking out on Man United’s ‘toxic culture’ [yesterday’s Football Daily, full email edition]. I broke out in a cold sweat reading about how they ‘give power to the players’. The stuff of nightmares, really” – Rowan Sweeney. Roberto De Zerbi wants Spurs to be a family ( yesterday’s Football Daily )? And he thinks playing for or with a family will avoid relegation? Well, I have this uncle. He’s called Weird Uncle Fiver (now there’s a throwback – Football Daily Ed), and he loves to [snip – Football Daily lawyers, and time-travelling pedants]” – Mike Wilner. item.content:encoded: Sign up now! Sign up now! Sign up now? Sign up now! Now then, which one of you hipsters decided to put Porto 0-1 PSV on? Oh dear. This was another night of Bigger Cup at its Bigliest self, comebacks everywhere, 40 goals in nine games, six of those in a best-v-best clash as Paris Saint-Germain rallied late against Barcelona. Even in defeat, Lamine Yamal found space to decorate the room with a ludicrous toe-poke equaliser, and there was a wholesome tale in Italy as Scott McTominay scored twice for Napoli in their 4-3 win against Bodø/Glimt. These were his first strikes since returning from heart surgery, taking his tally at the club to 29 goals in 86 appearances. No wonder Erik ten Hag was peeved with his bosses at Manchester United for shipping the midfielder off to Naples. One has to admire the courage of Erik ten Hag, speaking out on Man United’s ‘toxic culture’ [yesterday’s Football Daily, full email edition]. I broke out in a cold sweat reading about how they ‘give power to the players’. The stuff of nightmares, really” – Rowan Sweeney. Roberto De Zerbi wants Spurs to be a family ( yesterday’s Football Daily )? And he thinks playing for or with a family will avoid relegation? Well, I have this uncle. He’s called Weird Uncle Fiver (now there’s a throwback – Football Daily Ed), and he loves to [snip – Football Daily lawyers, and time-travelling pedants]” – Mike Wilner. item.title: Xbox's Official Shakeup Continues Through 2027 with New Rounds of Layoffs
item.description: The massive layoffs at Xbox Game Studios are far from over. Under new Xbox CEO Asha Sharma, the company has already cut 1,868 jobs since announcing in July that it would be reducing its headcount by 3,200 over the next year. Sharma is currently planning three additional rounds of layoffs for October, November, and January, according to a new report. Fortune noted that Xbox's layoffs have hit company veterans particularly hard, a move that is likely to erode institutional knowledge.

item.title: "A great budget lens for astrophotography, the sharpness produced at f/1.8 and f/2.8 is exactly what you want." Viltrox AF 16mm f/1.8 FE lens review
item.description: null Key specs Type: Full-frame prime lens Focal length: 16mm Maximum aperture: f/1.8 Lens mount: Sony FE, Nikon Z Weight: 19.4 oz (550 g) Dimensions: 3.35 x 4.06-in (85.2 x 103 mm) Filter thread: 77 mm Release date: May 2023 As you know, prime lenses come in a wide range of sizes and focal lengths, and every once in a while, one comes along and seems to grab you by the scruff of your neck. One such lens is the Viltrox AF 16mm f/1.8 FE, which is an impressive and useful lens for astrophotography thanks to its wide-angle field of view and fast maximum aperture. This lens is one of the wider prime lenses that are available and could be one of the best third-party lenses for astrophotography . With a price of just $464 (£533), this is one of the most cost-effective wide-angle primes, but rather than being a second-rate lens, its build quality and image quality are fantastic. It’s not the best, but it’s undoubtedly a lens you would enjoy. Image quality is excellent overall, with no need for lens corrections, except for vignette removal when shooting wide open. With near-perfect sharpness and minimal distortion and aberrations straight out of the camera, perhaps the weight of the lens is a small price to pay. The lens is made up of 15 elements in 12 groups and is built like a tank, with an all-metal body. It is pretty heavy, though, weighing in at 19.4 oz (550 g) despite its relatively compact size. Attach this lens to one of the best Sony cameras and you will have a formidable combination. The 16mm f/1.8 is also available in the Nikon Z-mount. Viltrox AF 16mm f/1.8 FE lens review Viltrox AF 16mm f/1.8 FE: Performance The Viltrox AF 16mm f/1.8 FE has a 77 mm filter thread. (Image credit: James Abbott) Great image quality Impressively sharp at f/1.8 Excellent corner sharpness With a focal length of 16mm and a maximum aperture of f/1.8, this is clearly a great lens for astrophotography from a technical point of view. The light-gathering capabilities are excellent, to say the least, and during testing it was possible to shoot at a range of ISO levels with a moonless sky. Even ISO 800 was often high enough for a correct exposure. The image quality produced by the 16mm f/1.8 is great, with excellent levels of sharpness across the frame. What’s most important here is that even corner sharpness is fantastic when wide open at f/1.8. This is the aperture setting where vignetting is at its strongest, but it reduces drastically when you stop down to f/2.8 and is completely gone by the time you stop down to f/4.
