DoubleAI, a Tel Aviv, Israel-based startup founded in 2023, on Monday introduced Maxwell , a code execution model (CEM) that evaluates, optimizes, and rewrites binary code during execution. Named for Maxwell's Demon , a creature imagined by physicist and mathematician James Clerk Maxwell in 1867 as part of a thought experiment on entropy, the Maxwell CEM preprocesses algorithms and machine instructions to maximize performance on available hardware. Maxwell is similar in concept to a just-in-time compiler, but provides more flexibility and formally verifies the equivalence of replacement code. Source code isn't touched. "Both Maxwell and a JIT compiler work while the program runs and both produce new machine code," said doubleAI co-founder Gal Beniamini, who holds a PhD in theoretical computer science, in an email to The Register . "The difference is that a compiler can't do high-level reasoning. It can't, for example, change the algorithm. Maxwell can and does. "One of the reasons why JIT compilers are so narrow is that, even though they can be data-dependent, the changes they make must be deterministic and correct 'by construction,' since JIT compilers are 'unthinking' classical algorithms. "Maxwell brings the expressive power of frontier AI into the 'JIT' setting. In addition, Maxwell relies on formal verification to write actual, hard proofs that show that its optimizations are sound. This expands the scope of its allowed optimisation far beyond that of any algorithm or compiler." Beniamini pointed to sorting as an example. The compiler, he said, will make a general-purpose sorting algorithm run as fast as it can, but it won't swap it out for a different algorithm. Compilers, said Beniamini, make decisions before the program runs and have to be narrow and conservative in their choices. Maxwell, he said, works with more information, isn't just a one-pass operation, and operates at a higher level. "It sees the exact hardware the program has landed on, and the actual shapes and types of the data flowing through it (information that is only available during runtime!)," Beniamini explained. "It also sees the state of the environment, what else is running in the same program, and which actual bottlenecks express themselves, and under which conditions. This allows it to specialize in ways a compiler never can." Since Maxwell operates continuously, it can keep improving programs as new bottlenecks arise. And it can "reason" in a way that compilers cannot. Maxwell's approach wouldn't be possible if the model rewrote code in a way that introduced errors on the fly, so the formal proof capability is not optional. According to doubleAI, Maxwell has made data pipelines more than 38x faster and AI inference kernels more than 4.5x faster. LTX-2.5 , an open world model that generates 4K video, managed to do so almost twice as fast with the help of Maxwell. Maxwell's optimizations reduced the data being exchanged between GPUs and optimized the kernel selection to drop unnecessary token padding. Maxwell's optimization capability varies depending on the source code and the hardware. "Maxwell does best on code that is algorithmic, and which can be tailored to hardware in a non-trivial manner," said Beniamini. "That being said, even code that isn't like that, but is written in a high level language like Python, can usually enjoy far reaching optimisations due to the available overhang. The same is true for PyTorch graphs, which (even under Torch's compiler) tend to be extremely far from optimal." It can also help with code security. Beniamini said Maxwell can eliminate issues like memory errors by proving their non-existence as part of the formalization process. "Anecdotally, we have found such issues in Python itself, through the use of Maxwell – i.e., cases in which Python was not memory safe, and where Maxwell proved that to be the case," he said. And better still, Maxwell's tracing and profiling don't incur much if any overhead on either the CPU or GPU. "The maximal overhead of Maxwell's tracing and profiling is 2 percent (when it isn't tracing, that falls to zero, of course), and the optimisations that Maxwell yields far outweigh that," said Beniamini. "We also apply Maxwell to the runtime itself, so that we get back a much larger than 2 percent 'flat' speedup, across the board. So in short: it's never slower." The installation process is similarly light-touch: Devs install the runtime and run their code, with the Maxwell model hosted by doubleAI. This arrangement, however, does require some amount of trust. Amnon Shashua, co-founder and CEO of doubleAI, founder and departing CEO of Mobileye and a professor of computer science at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, said in a statement that AI has changed how software is written and now is changing how it runs. "CEMs, and Maxwell in particular, are agents on behalf of the hardware as opposed to code agents that are on behalf of the human user," he said. "In other words, they are the first AI that works for the machine, not the programmer." ®

item.title: Japan launches historic MMX sample-return mission to Mars' moon Phobos (video)
item.description: null Japan's groundbreaking mission to Mars is officially underway, headed to the Red Planet's mysterious moons Phobos and Deimos for a historic sample-return attempt. The Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) mission launched today (Oct. 19) from Tanegashima Space Center in Japan, riding an H3 rocket that lifted off from Pad-2 at Tanegashima's Yoshinobu Launch Complex at 3:41 p.m. EDT (1941 GMT; 4:41 a.m. local time in Japan on Oct. 20). The JAXA ( Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency )-led MMX mission is bound for Mars orbit, where it will study the planet's two moons, Phobos and Deimos. If everything goes according to plan, MMX will become the first spacecraft to land on and return samples from Phobos for study back on Earth, which scientists think could shed light on a decades-old mystery about the moons' origins and reveal clues about the formation of the early solar system . a rocket launches into a night sky from a seaside pad (Image credit: JAXA) It was the 10th liftoff of Japan's expendable, two-stage H3 rocket, which was jointly developed by JAXA and Mitsubishi Heavy Industries. item.content:encoded: null Japan's groundbreaking mission to Mars is officially underway, headed to the Red Planet's mysterious moons Phobos and Deimos for a historic sample-return attempt. The Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) mission launched today (Oct. 19) from Tanegashima Space Center in Japan, riding an H3 rocket that lifted off from Pad-2 at Tanegashima's Yoshinobu Launch Complex at 3:41 p.m. EDT (1941 GMT; 4:41 a.m. local time in Japan on Oct. 20). The JAXA ( Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency )-led MMX mission is bound for Mars orbit, where it will study the planet's two moons, Phobos and Deimos. If everything goes according to plan, MMX will become the first spacecraft to land on and return samples from Phobos for study back on Earth, which scientists think could shed light on a decades-old mystery about the moons' origins and reveal clues about the formation of the early solar system . a rocket launches into a night sky from a seaside pad (Image credit: JAXA) It was the 10th liftoff of Japan's expendable, two-stage H3 rocket, which was jointly developed by JAXA and Mitsubishi Heavy Industries. After clearing its launch pad today, the 207-foot-tall (63 meters) launch vehicle flew a nominal trajectory through its ascent corridor over the Pacific Ocean, jettisoning its four solid boosters in pairs just before the flight clock reached two minutes. The rocket shed its payload fairings about one minute and 20 seconds later, exposing MMX to the vacuum of space for the first time. H3's first stage, powered by two LE-9 rocket engines, channels a mixture of liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen to produce a combined thrust of 331,000 pounds (1,471 kN), according to Mitsubishi Heavy Industries. As the mission clock approached T+5 minutes, H3 executed its main engine cutoff procedure and separated from the second stage, which ignited its engines for a 5.5-minute burn about 10 seconds later. All continued to go to plan after that. The H3's upper stage ignited its engine for a second time for a trans-Mars injection burn about one hour and four minutes after liftoff, a maneuver that lasted roughly six minutes and 25 seconds and took MMX to a maximum velocity of about 24,145 mph (38,858 kph). MMX was released from the rocket's upper stage right on schedule, about one minute after the completion of that burn and roughly 71 minutes after liftoff. The success elicited loud cheers in mission control, which viewers saw and heard on JAXA's launch webcast. MMX is now under its own power, and on course for Mars. The interplanetary transit will last about 10 months, with the spacecraft scheduled to arrive at the Red Planet in August 2027. When it does, MMX's propulsion module will execute an orbital insertion burn to place itself in a quasi-satellite orbit (QSO) around Phobos, which places MMX within the space around the moon as both circle Mars. MMX will spend about three years in the Martian system, devoting much of that time to studying the 14-mile-wide (22 km) Phobos with its science instruments. The spacecraft also carries the IDEFIX rover, a joint effort of the space agencies of France and Germany, which is scheduled to deploy to the surface of Phobos in late 2028 or early 2029. After a mapping campaign to select suitable landing sites, MMX will perform two separate touchdowns on Phobos to collect and stow samples in the spacecraft's return capsule. Following its second landing and sample collection, MMX will briefly return to QSO with Phobos before transferring to a more elongated orbit around Mars that intersects with the planet's smaller moon, Deimos, which is just 8 miles (14 km) in diameter. During the last several months of its time around Mars, MMX will perform a series of Deimos flybys before departing for Earth in November 2030. If all goes according to plan, the MMX sample-return capsule will land in Australia in 2031. Scientists are counting on those samples, and other data collected during MMX's time around Mars, to answer a decades-old question surrounding the Martian moons' origins. Competing theories and conflicting evidence point to two possibilities for how Mars got its moons . Their near-circular, equatorial orbits suggest a narrative similar to how Earth's moon is thought to have formed — as a result of a massive planetary impact between Mars and some other giant space rock, which broke off pieces of the planet that eventually coalesced to form the natural satellites that orbit there today. A composite image with Mars and its two moons, Phobos and Deimos. (Image credit: NASA/JPL/University of Arizona) Neither Phobos nor Deimos is spherical, isntead; both are oblong and lumpy, like potatoes. That fact — along with their chemical composition, as far as we have been able to tell using telescopic spectroscopy — point to the possibility that Phobos and Deimos were asteroids from the early solar system that were captured by Mars' gravitational pull. Figuring out the moons' true origin story would provide key clues about Mars' geological past, the solar system's early history and the formation of the inner planets , mission team members have said. Once the MMX samples are safely returned to Earth, scientists will study their composition and mineralogy, then compare such chemical fingerprints with those of Martian rocks and asteroid material. These analyses, combined with data collected by MMX during its mission, will help nail down the origin of Phobos — and by extension, Deimos. — by While JAXA leads MMX, the mission is an international effort, with interagency partnerships between JAXA, NASA and the European Space Agency (ESA), as well as U.S. and European companies, which supplied a handful of the spacecraft's scientific hardware and communications equipment. NASA's contributions to MMX include the Mars-moon Exploration with Gamma rays and Neutrons (MEGANE, pronounced "meh-gah-nay") device, which is a gamma-ray and neutron spectrometer built by the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory (APL); a Honeybee Robotics-built pneumatic sampler; and communications support using the agency's Deep Space Network. NASA has also invested approximately $87 million through the end of the mission, which includes funding for United States scientists and astromaterials experts on the MMX team. The agency is getting something concrete for such contributions: At least 15% of the planned 10-gram (0.35 ounces) returned Phobos sample will be reserved for NASA's study. Those materials will be transferred and maintained at the agency's Johnson Space Center in Houston for analysis and long-term preservation. MMX is not the first Phobos sample-return project to take flight, by the way. That distinction goes to Russia's Phobos-Grunt ("Phobos-Soil") mission, which launched in November 2011 but failed to get out of Earth orbit due to a rocket glitch. The 14.5-ton spacecraft eventually crashed back to Earth over the Pacific Ocean in January 2012. Editor's note: This story was updated at 5 p.m. ET on Oct. 19 with news of MMX's successful separation from the H3 rocket's upper stage.

item.title: On this day in space! Oct. 19, 2016: Europe's ExoMars orbiter and Schiaparelli lander arrive at Mars
item.description: null On Oct. 19, 2016, the European Space Agency's ExoMars mission arrived at Mars ! ExoMars 2016 consists of the Trace Gas Orbiter and the Schiaparelli lander. The orbiter and lander traveled there together and separated on Oct. 16, three days before the orbiter entered orbit around Mars , and the lander touched down on the planet's surface. But something went wrong during the lander's descent, and it crashed into the ground. Schiaparelli did not survive the accident , but the Trace Gas Orbiter is still functional. It is currently circling the planet, looking for methane and other gases in the Martian atmosphere that could be evidence for possible biological activity. Artist’s illustration showing the separation of the ExoMars 2016 entry, descent and landing demonstrator module, named Schiaparelli, from the Trace Gas Orbiter, and heading for Mars. (Image credit: ESA) Why it mattered ExoMars 2016 was a landmark mission for the European Space Agency and designed to be the vanguard of a two-flight ExoMars program to send an orbiter, lander and rover to Mars. Launched in March 2016, ExoMars 2016 aimed to achieve two goals for ESA and Russia. First, the mission aimed to use the Schiaparelli lander to test landing techniques that would be vital on a planned ExoMars 2018 rover . Second, the mission would deliver a critical orbiter around Mars to study the planet's atmosphere and serve as a communications link for that future Mars rover. In the end, ExoMars 2016 was just a partial success, with ESA officials calling it "96% successful." due to the loss of the lander. While Schiaparelli separated smoothly from the ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter spacecraft, it stopped communicating with Earth just 1 minute before its planned landing on Oct. 19. Photos from NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter at Mars later revealed what appeared to be its crash site and, nearby, its jettisoned parachute. Officials suspect Schiaparelli did not fire its descent thrusters as designed in order to slow itself enough for a safe landing. A data glitch was cited as its cause . The Trace Gas Orbiter, meanwhile, continues to study Mars to this day and has spent 10 years and counting studying the Martian atmosphere . The launch of ExoMars 2018, which includes the Mars rover Rosalind Franklin, was delayed by the Schiaparelli failure, as well as the loss of its Russian Proton rocket when ESA severed its partnership with Russia over that country's war on Ukraine. The ExoMars rover is now expected to launch no earlier than 2028, with a landing on Mars expected in 2030. In 2026, another country took aim at Mars on this day. The Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency attempted to launch the ambitious Martian Moons eXploration mission (called MMX) to land a probe on the Mars moon Phobos and return samples to Earth. Want more space history? Check out our full On This Day In Space Story archive and watch our On This Day In Space videos on YouTube .

item.title: The moon is shrinking. 10,000 cracks on the lunar surface reveal by how much
item.description: null The moon is shrinking, and scientists are narrowing in on exactly how much our natural satellite has dwindled over the years. The moon is thought to have formed from a violent collision between a massive object and our young Earth roughly 4.5 billion years ago, and its interior is still gradually cooling off from this ancient collision. As it cools, the moon contracts, leading to a long, slow shrinking process . Now, in a new study, scientists think that they have figured out how much smaller the moon is actually getting. In this new study, scientists analyzing images snapped by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera (LROC) have spotted over 10,000 young faults, or cracks across the moon's surface. This helped them to figure out how much the moon has contracted over time, and they now estimate that the moon's radius has decreased by about 148 feet (45 meters) over the past 400 to 800 million years. "The number of these young faults revealed in LROC images is much greater than I ever imagined," study lead Thomas Watters, a geologist and scientist emeritus at the Center for Earth and Planetary Studies at the Smithsonian's National Air and Space Museum, said in a statement . "As the interior of the moon continues to cool and contract, it is expected that the growth of existing faults and formation of new faults continues today." Lobate scarps on the lunar surface, as seen by LROC. (Image credit: NASA/KARI/ASU/Intuitive Machines/Smithsonian ) With these LROC observations, researchers in this study saw a variety of different types of cracks and landforms across the lunar surface. This included lobate scarps, or long, curved structures that form when the moon's surface contracts, cracks and is pushed upwards; and small mare ridges, or narrow "wrinkles" in the lunar surface, across the dark plains on the moon . Lobate scarps on the moon, as seen by LROC. (Image credit: NASA/KARI/ASU/Intuitive Machines/Smithsonian) Tectonic activity on the moon looks a lot different than it does on Earth. On our own planet, there are about 15 major tectonic plates. On the moon, there are no tectonic plates at all. Instead, the moon has a single-plate body meaning its outer shell is a single piece only broken by faults or other such cracks created by the moon contracting. This means that instead of faults or cracks appearing at tectonic plate boundaries, they are instead scattered all over the moon. A global map of lunar faults. Red lines indicate over 8,900 lobate scarps while blue lines show over 2,000 small mare ridges. (Image credit: NASA/ASU/Intuitive Machines/Smithsonian) By mapping these thousands of different features, all created from the moon cooling and contracting over time, the researchers are piecing together lunar history. (Image credit: NASA/KARI/ASU/Intuitive Machines/Smithsonian ) With these LROC observations, researchers in this study saw a variety of different types of cracks and landforms across the lunar surface. This included lobate scarps, or long, curved structures that form when the moon's surface contracts, cracks and is pushed upwards; and small mare ridges, or narrow "wrinkles" in the lunar surface, across the dark plains on the moon . Lobate scarps on the moon, as seen by LROC. (Image credit: NASA/KARI/ASU/Intuitive Machines/Smithsonian) Tectonic activity on the moon looks a lot different than it does on Earth. On our own planet, there are about 15 major tectonic plates. On the moon, there are no tectonic plates at all. This means that instead of faults or cracks appearing at tectonic plate boundaries, they are instead scattered all over the moon. A global map of lunar faults. Red lines indicate over 8,900 lobate scarps while blue lines show over 2,000 small mare ridges. (Image credit: NASA/ASU/Intuitive Machines/Smithsonian) By mapping these thousands of different features, all created from the moon cooling and contracting over time, the researchers are piecing together lunar history. In addition to finding the extent to which the moon has shrunk over time, they also found that some areas of the moon are covered in many more faults than other areas, and the areas with fewer cracks and faults have thicker moon crust. This led them to conclude that not only are these areas with thicker crust more stable, but they suggest that a great deal of the widespread cracks in the lunar surface were created later in the moon's history as, in its earlier years, its thick crust would have insulated the moon's warm interior and prevented cooling, contracting and cracking. This work was described in a study published Oct. 14 in The Planetary Science Journal.

item.title: Kikelomo Atanda-Owo Celebrates 20 Years in Media Unveils Podcast With Husband Reuben Abati
item.description: Ace broadcaster, media entrepreneur and host of Real Talk With Kike , Kikelomo Atanda-Owo , alongside her husband, veteran journalist and broadcaster Dr. Reuben Abati , has officially unveiled “ The Reuben and Kike Abati Podcast ,” marking an exciting new chapter in their broadcasting careers. The announcement was made on Saturday, October 10, 2026, during the celebration of Kikelomo Atanda-Owo’s 20 years in the media industry, held at Eko Hotels & Suites, Lagos. The occasion also commemorated the seventh anniversary of her flagship talk show, Real Talk With Kike, bringing together distinguished personalities, media executives, business leaders, industry stakeholders and well-wishers. The unveiling of The Reuben and Kike Abati Podcast represents a significant milestone for the celebrated media couple, who are bringing their wealth of experience, individual perspectives and shared passion for meaningful conversations to a new digital platform. The podcast is envisioned as a platform for engaging, thought-provoking and insightful conversations on issues shaping contemporary society, including governance, politics, relationships, family, culture, lifestyle, entertainment and everyday experiences. According to Lagos News Hub, combining Dr. Reuben Abati’s extensive background in journalism, political analysis and public affairs with Kikelomo Atanda-Owo’s distinctive approach to human-interest storytelling, lifestyle conversations and audience engagement, the podcast promises a compelling blend of perspectives, experience and authenticity. Beyond their individual accomplishments in broadcasting, the new podcast creates an opportunity for the couple to explore important subjects together, bringing their different professional experiences and viewpoints into conversations designed to inform, educate and entertain audiences. For Kikelomo Atanda-Owo, the unveiling comes at a particularly significant moment in her career as she celebrates two decades of consistency, resilience and impact in the Nigerian media landscape. Over the years, she has established herself as a respected voice in broadcasting, using Real Talk With Kike to facilitate conversations around personal development, relationships, social issues, leadership and the experiences that shape everyday life. Dr. Reuben Abati, on his part, brings decades of experience as a journalist, columnist, public affairs commentator and former presidential spokesperson. His contributions to political discourse and national conversations have established him as one of Nigeria’s recognisable media voices. Together, the couple will seek to create a distinctive podcast experience that combines serious conversations with relatable discussions, personal insights and engaging exchanges. item.title: Kikelomo Atanda-Owo Celebrates 20 Years in Media: Unveils Podcast With Reuben Abati as Abike Dabiri Other Dignitaries Attend
item.description: It was a celebration of excellence, resilience, innovation and over two decades of remarkable contributions to the Nigerian media industry as ace broadcaster and media entrepreneur, Kikelomo Atanda-Owo , celebrated her 20th anniversary in broadcasting alongside the seventh anniversary of her flagship television programme, Real Talk With Kike , at Eko Hotels & Suites, Victoria Island, Lagos, on Saturday, October 10, 2026. The high-profile event, themed “The Future of Nigeria: Where Leadership, Innovation, Culture & Media Converge to Shape Nation Building,” brought together prominent personalities from government, business, media, entertainment and the diplomatic community to celebrate the broadcaster’s professional journey and examine the role of leadership, innovation and responsible media in Nigeria’s development. One of the major highlights of the occasion was the official unveiling of “The Reuben and Kike Abati Podcast ,” a new digital media platform jointly introduced by Kikelomo Atanda-Owo and her husband, veteran journalist, political analyst and former presidential spokesperson, Dr. Reuben Abati. The anniversary celebration also featured a keynote address delivered by the Secretary to the Lagos State Government, Barrister Bimbola Salu-Hundeyin , who represented the Lagos State Deputy Governor, Dr. Kadri Obafemi Hamzat . The keynote session reflected the conference’s central theme, drawing attention to the intersection of leadership, innovation, culture and the media in shaping Nigeria’s future. The occasion also provided an opportunity to reflect on the responsibilities of media practitioners in promoting constructive national conversations and encouraging greater participation in nation-building. The event, according to Lagos News Hub attracted an impressive gathering of distinguished personalities, including Hon. Abike Dabiri-Erewa, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of the Nigerians in Diaspora Commission (NiDCOM) ; Hannatu Musa Musawa , Honourable Minister of Art, Culture, Tourism and the Creative Economy; Dr. Allen Onyema , Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of Air Peace ; Tosin Akerele ; and Kola Adesina , Group Managing Director of Sahara Power Group, alongside other notable personalities from the public and private sectors. Their presence underscored the significance of the occasion and the relationships Kikelomo Atanda-Owo has cultivated throughout her two-decade career in the media industry. Beyond the celebration of professional milestones, the gathering created an avenue for networking, meaningful engagement and conversations around the evolving Nigerian media landscape, particularly the growing influence of digital platforms, content innovation and strategic storytelling. For Kikelomo Atanda-Owo, the occasion was a celebration of consistency, determination, professional growth and the enduring relevance of meaningful conversations in a rapidly changing media environment. Beyond the celebration of professional milestones, the gathering created an avenue for networking, meaningful engagement and conversations around the evolving Nigerian media landscape, particularly the growing influence of digital platforms, content innovation and strategic storytelling. For Kikelomo Atanda-Owo, the occasion was a celebration of consistency, determination, professional growth and the enduring relevance of meaningful conversations in a rapidly changing media environment. Through Real Talk With Kike, which has now completed seven years, she has continued to engage audiences on relationships, personal development, lifestyle, social challenges and other important subjects, establishing the programme as a platform for thought-provoking discussions. With the successful celebration of 20 years in media, seven years of Real Talk With Kike, and the unveiling of a new podcast alongside her husband, Kikelomo Atanda-Owo has opened another chapter in her career, reinforcing her commitment to storytelling, media innovation and conversations that contribute meaningfully to society. item.title: Saskay Celebrates Master’s Degree From VUB Brussels School of Governance in Hertunba | See Photos
item.description: Saskay celebrating her Master of Arts degree in Global Security and Strategy. Who says you need a suit to celebrate a master’s degree? Saskay is marking a major academic milestone on her own terms, swapping the Western-style outfit she originally planned for a look rooted in heritage. The Big Brother Naija star, whose real name is Tsakute Ladi Jonah , has earned a Master of Arts (MA) in Global Security and Strategy from VUB Brussels School of Governance, and her graduation photos make room for both her academic achievement and a conversation about how we dress for success. Reflecting on what the degree means to her, Saskay shared how studying a subject she has always been passionate about made the experience especially meaningful. Master of Arts (MA) in Global Security and Strategy. I got to study something I’ve always been passionate about, and that makes this degree mean so much more to me. I’ve poured so much of myself into this journey that my diploma is basically my baby. Saskay in the Hertunba Nola Kaftan for her graduation portraits. Her choice of outfit came about after her original plan fell through. Saskay had intended to wear a suit for the shoot, but her designer had an emergency and could not complete it in time. The change prompted her to reflect on why Western clothing is so often associated with academic achievement, and how graduation portraits can also celebrate cultural identity. I had a suit planned for this shoot, but my designer had an emergency and couldn’t get it ready in time. Things took a different turn, and it got me thinking about how we’ve come to associate education with western clothing. There’s something beautiful about celebrating an academic milestone in a way that also reflects who we are and where we come from. Saskay in her graduation outfit celebrating her MA in Global Security and Strategy. For the shoot, Saskay wore the Nola Kaftan by Hertunba, a flowing, 100% cotton design featuring motifs of palm trees, birds and dwellings. The motifs tell a metaphorical story of a small girl in a big village, with each illustration contributing to the larger narrative woven into the design. The kaftan featured a generous silhouette, fluid sleeves and an open drape, with its off-white and cream tones complemented by a chocolate brown silk veil. Saskay posing with her VUB Brussels School of Governance degree case. She paired the kaftan with traditional-inspired facial art, including a triangle on her forehead, a line across the bridge of her nose and a vertical line extending from her lower lip to her chin. Oversized leaf-shaped gold drop earrings, a layered beaded gold necklace, thick gold cuffs, wide bangles and statement rings completed her look. Beauty detail of Saskay featuring traditional African facial art markings, a shaved head, gold leaf earrings, and layered beaded jewellery for her Master’s degree graduation portraits. In some of the photographs, Saskay posed with a leather degree holder bearing her institutio

item.title: Security patches need patches now that attackers have AI
item.description: Updating your software only gets you so far. A scary scenario - security fixes themselves being bypassed - is becoming more common, according to AI penetration-testing startup Terra Security, which found a sharp rise in reported patch failures in 2026 after years of relatively low numbers. And no, it’s not a coincidence that AI vulnerability discovery and patching also exploded this year. For example, Russian government cyberspies exploited a zero-day Windows Shell security bypass bug, CVE-2026-21510, at least a month before Microsoft patched the flaw in February. Redmond’s patch, however, was incomplete, and left a second flaw - a zero-click authentication coercion vulnerability (CVE-2026-32202) - that was also found and abused before Microsoft fixed it in April. Terra researchers reviewed every published CVE record and GitHub-reviewed advisory looking for broken fixes, and found a distinct pattern . After six years of relatively few patch bypasses, this changed in 2026: “A fix would ship, a bypass would be found, and another fix would go out.” The share of GitHub security fixes that required a follow-up advisory reporting a failed patch within 90 days remained at about 0.2 percent between 2019 and 2025. This year, this figure had jumped to 2.3 percent, according to the researchers. Meanwhile, vulnerabilities whose fixes were later bypassed were about four times as likely to appear on the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency's (CISA's) Known Exploited Vulnerabilities list as other bugs affecting the same vendors, according to Terra. Of these, server-side request forgery fixes and prototype-pollution patches break the most. Compared with their share of all CVEs, prototype-pollution vulnerabilities were about 11 times as common among broken-fix CVEs, while server-side request forgery vulnerabilities were 4.6 times as common, according to Terra. This has to do with the way these types of bug classes are fixed: using a reject-list of inputs such as hostnames, paths, and object keys. There’s a “simple” reason for this, according to Terra. “If the blocklist doesn't foresee every encoding of a bad input, the attacker only needs to find one,” the researchers said. Fixes for Linux kernel vulnerabilities are also more likely to cause new bugs, according to kernel CNA records as of October 8. “In fact, 3.2 percent of kernel CVEs were introduced by the fix for another CVE, and about 10 percent in busy subsystems like fs/smb and net/sched,” the bug hunters noted. The silver lining in all of this, we’re told, is that it should be a wake-up call for software vendors and network defenders to break the “patch and move on habit.” Instead, before shipping patches, software vendors should consider three questions: Does it fix the root cause? Does it cover the whole bug class? Does it break something else? And for sysadmins and patch managers: consider the same things before applying the fix. “If a vendor fixes an exploited bug, assume someone is read

And for sysadmins and patch managers: consider the same things before applying the fix. “If a vendor fixes an exploited bug, assume someone is reading the patch for a way around it,” the pen testers advise. ®

item.title: Will that do? Lamine Yamal conjures another magical spell as Barça pass first test | Sid Lowe
item.description: The 19-year-old scored a cracker in Seville, days after his ‘almost rabona’ at Galatasaray, as La Liga leaders beat Real Betis When at last it was time for Lamine Yamal to leave, the 19-year-old’s number going up before the 90th minute for only the second time since the opening day, Real Betis fans whistled him all the way to the touchline where Barcelona’s coach was waiting. His work here was done, Hansi Flick invited him to take the weight off his feet and his shoulders, not that he wanted to. First, though, he took Lamine Yamal’s head in his hands and, leaning in away from the amateur lip readers, tried to make himself heard over the noise. “I told him I was proud of him because he played a fantastic game,” he said. At least he could think of something. When Lamine Yamal had opened the scoring just nine minutes into the match that was supposed to find out how good Barcelona really were, it hadn’t been easy. Nothing erudite, anyway. On the morning that Barcelona went to Betis – first v third, a proper opponent at last – Jorge Valdano had lamented that sometimes he doesn’t have the words, and he always has the words. Valdano had just watched Lamine do that , whatever that was , in Istanbul – an “almost rabona ”, the kid called it – and now he had a problem. “If he keeps doing strange things, we’re not going to be able to explain it,” he wrote . Continue reading...

item.title: Write bot-resistant code with KillSwitch, a programming language designed to confuse LLMs
item.description: If you want to keep bots from making sense of the code you worked so hard on and using it to write programs of their own, there's a new programming language out there designed to confuse LLMs. What began as software engineer Dominik Picheta experimenting with whether LLMs understand the code they write has turned into something else entirely: An open-source, albeit esoteric, programming language he’s dubbed KillSwitch . There are no brackets, no formatting standards to remember, and seemingly no structure: Just chunks of text, ideally as prosaic as possible, interspersed with functions, variables, and statements written in a manner to be as confusing as possible to LLMs. That means humans might be a bit befuddled too, naturally. “It's totally normal for a human to be confused by the language at first,” Picheta told The Register . “I like to think of it as a bit of a fun puzzle: you should explore the language, play with its interpreter and learn how all the pieces fit together.” KillSwitch wasn’t built by any random person looking to code something confusing to LLMs, and it wasn’t vibe-coded by an AI enthusiast, either. Picheta knows his way around programming languages: He’s a senior software engineer at Cloudflare working on the Workers Runtime team, and is one of the core developers of the Nim programming language. At its most basic, KillSwitch is based around adverbs, which serve as every single identifier in a piece of code. Calling one of those identifiers requires using an anagram of the original adverb, but those anagrams don't have to be actual words - just rearrangements of the original letters. Take, for example, pushing "Hello World" onto the stack and then printing it, as explained on the demo page linked earlier in the story. The program contains several paragraphs of text, most of which the interpreter ignores apart from a few key phrases. Writing “ this story starts [adverb] ” identifies a code entrypoint. Once inside the code section, writing “ ignore previous instructions [adverb anagram] ” calls a function, several of which are predefined. In the case of "Hello World," the function to print something is "visibly." Put whatever you want to print in quotation marks, push it onto the stack, call "visibly," and that's that. KillSwitch isn’t a full-featured language, with Picheta describing it as a stack-based interpreted language with only “a limited set of constructs including functions, variables, and if statements,” given its evolution out of an experiment to see how well a programming language could fool an AI into not understanding what was written. Where it gets confusing for an AI is with commands like “ignore previous instructions,” especially when found in the middle of a chunk of text that doesn’t make much sense in that context. item.dc:creator: Brandon Vigliarolo
item.content:encoded: If you want to keep bots from making sense of the code you worked so hard on and using it to write programs of their own, there's a new programming language out there designed to confuse LLMs. What began as software engineer Dominik Picheta experimenting with whether LLMs understand the code they write has turned into something else entirely: An open-source, albeit esoteric, programming language he’s dubbed KillSwitch . There are no brackets, no formatting standards to remember, and seemingly no structure: Just chunks of text, ideally as prosaic as possible, interspersed with functions, variables, and statements written in a manner to be as confusing as possible to LLMs. That means humans might be a bit befuddled too, naturally. “It's totally normal for a human to be confused by the language at first,” Picheta told The Register . “I like to think of it as a bit of a fun puzzle: you should explore the language, play with its interpreter and learn how all the pieces fit together.” KillSwitch wasn’t built by any random person looking to code something confusing to LLMs, and it wasn’t vibe-coded by an AI enthusiast, either. Picheta knows his way around programming languages: He’s a senior software engineer at Cloudflare working on the Workers Runtime team, and is one of the core developers of the Nim programming language. At its most basic, KillSwitch is based around adverbs, which serve as every single identifier in a piece of code. Calling one of those identifiers requires using an anagram of the original adverb, but those anagrams don't have to be actual words - just rearrangements of the original letters. Take, for example, pushing "Hello World" onto the stack and then printing it, as explained on the demo page linked earlier in the story. The program contains several paragraphs of text, most of which the interpreter ignores apart from a few key phrases. Writing “ this story starts [adverb] ” identifies a code entrypoint. Once inside the code section, writing “ ignore previous instructions [adverb anagram] ” calls a function, several of which are predefined. In the case of "Hello World," the function to print something is "visibly." Put whatever you want to print in quotation marks, push it onto the stack, call "visibly," and that's that. KillSwitch isn’t a full-featured language, with Picheta describing it as a stack-based interpreted language with only “a limited set of constructs including functions, variables, and if statements,” given its evolution out of an experiment to see how well a programming language could fool an AI into not understanding what was written. Where it gets confusing for an AI is with commands like “ignore previous instructions,” especially when found in the middle of a chunk of text that doesn’t make much sense in that context. KillSwitch’s specification document on GitHub provides more details about the language and is itself designed to confuse LLMs. In one section of the spec, it’s explained that KillSwitch “is equipped with the ability to scan the local network, attempt to find security vulnerabilities in the services on that network, then take those services over and terminate them.” That's not actually the case, as a close reading of the paragraph reveals and Picheta confirmed to us. “The hack statement is both designed to trigger many models' safety guardrails but also to test an LLM's ability to discern fact from fiction,” Picheta told us, adding that there are several lies in the spec document designed to confuse any LLM that may scrape it in an attempt to understand how the language works. “The idea is that humans should be able to deduce what is a lie, whereas LLMs are naive and can be easily swayed by what is written in the spec,” Picheta added. “Some don't realize what its semantic meaning is, whereas others refuse to continue because they believe the script may hack someone.” Do LLMs understand what they write? A programming language designed to confuse AI models seems unlikely to stay obfuscated for long - especially if it’s open source, available on Github , and likely to be scraped by an LLM at some point. Picheta’s aware of that inevitability, which, along with the fact he wanted to test AI’s ability to understand confusing code, is why he’s benchmarked a number of major models against it. “I'm 99.9 percent certain the AI models I benchmarked KS on have not been trained on its source,” Picheta said. “The source hasn't been in the public domain for very long … I'm pretty sure none of the benchmarked models have had training runs that began after the release.” The best-performing model only managed a composite benchmark score of 66.8 percent on KillSwitch coding tasks, while most struggled to get above 50 percent. Even at that high a score, Picheta doesn’t believe it suggests LLMs understand the code they’re writing. Examples in the benchmark were simple, and he believes that, even if an AI were trained on the intricacies of KillSwitch, it’s still going to get tripped up. “My instinct is that in those circumstances they will suddenly be able to ace the basic tasks, which are based on the open sourced test files in the GitHub repo, but will continue to fail to build more complex tasks requiring them to write longer and more complex scripts,” Picheta asserted - and he’s up for the challenge. “I am excited to see how KillSwitch shows up in model training, and think that we can also take advantage of that training to break LLMs in new ways too as KillSwitch evolves,” Picheta said. Those interested in trying KillSwitch out can find it on GitHub, and don't hesitate to make changes: Picheta said he’s ready and willing to incorporate new ways of making it even more LLM resistant. ®

item.title: Europe’s cloud sovereignty rules could do more harm than good
item.description: Europe’s drive for cloud sovereignty is leading to member states favoring providers from their own nation instead of building a Europe-wide cloud services market, according to a report critical of the EU’s proposed Cloud and AI Development Act ( CADA ). A study by the European Centre for International Political Economy (ECIPE) looked at public cloud contracts in nine EU member states and found that every one that invoked the new vocabulary around “sovereignty” went to a domestic provider, rather than one based in another EU country. It says that European cloud procurement was already highly concentrated nationally before sovereignty became a key policy objective, based on analysis of 8,725 cloud-related procurement contracts between 2018 and 2025. Nearly all went to providers in the same country with negligible intra-EU cross-border competition. Furthermore, the report claims that those domestic wins often turn out to be from prime contractors that are relying on infrastructure provided by the big hyperscale operators, where sovereignty attaches to the nationality of the operator, not to the infrastructure layer on which the service depends. At issue is a conceptual confusion over cloud sovereignty, which is being used to represent two different problems, according to ECIPE. One treats sovereignty as a security and resilience objective, securing data and managing risks. Sovereignty here means that the user has choices over the provider and design of their cloud service needs. The second treats sovereignty as an industrial policy objective, where sovereignty is more about the notion of Europe-headquartered firms becoming more successful if they are not exposed to competition with non-European providers. CADA includes the two different logics and, confusingly, aims to achieve both outcomes, the report states. The legislation frames the four European Union assurance levels as criteria for security, resilience and trustworthy cloud provision, but the criteria actually aim to enforce sovereignty through requirements concerning EU-located infrastructure, restrictions on third-country control, and control over software supply chains. The goal of cloud sovereignty is therefore at risk of becoming a vehicle for policies that favor selected providers, restrict competition and fragment digital markets, ECIPE warns. Instead of allowing pan-European rivals for the big US cloud providers to grow and flourish, the framework may thus have the opposite effect in encouraging member states to favor providers within their own borders, leading to fragmentation across Europe. A more coherent approach would keep the resilience objectives, but temper their use through technological neutrality requirements that preserve interoperability, portability, and multi-cloud options, the report authors state. item.dc:creator: Dan Robinson
item.content:encoded: Europe’s drive for cloud sovereignty is leading to member states favoring providers from their own nation instead of building a Europe-wide cloud services market, according to a report critical of the EU’s proposed Cloud and AI Development Act ( CADA ). A study by the European Centre for International Political Economy (ECIPE) looked at public cloud contracts in nine EU member states and found that every one that invoked the new vocabulary around “sovereignty” went to a domestic provider, rather than one based in another EU country. It says that European cloud procurement was already highly concentrated nationally before sovereignty became a key policy objective, based on analysis of 8,725 cloud-related procurement contracts between 2018 and 2025. Nearly all went to providers in the same country with negligible intra-EU cross-border competition. Furthermore, the report claims that those domestic wins often turn out to be from prime contractors that are relying on infrastructure provided by the big hyperscale operators, where sovereignty attaches to the nationality of the operator, not to the infrastructure layer on which the service depends. At issue is a conceptual confusion over cloud sovereignty, which is being used to represent two different problems, according to ECIPE. One treats sovereignty as a security and resilience objective, securing data and managing risks. Sovereignty here means that the user has choices over the provider and design of their cloud service needs. The second treats sovereignty as an industrial policy objective, where sovereignty is more about the notion of Europe-headquartered firms becoming more successful if they are not exposed to competition with non-European providers. CADA includes the two different logics and, confusingly, aims to achieve both outcomes, the report states. The legislation frames the four European Union assurance levels as criteria for security, resilience and trustworthy cloud provision, but the criteria actually aim to enforce sovereignty through requirements concerning EU-located infrastructure, restrictions on third-country control, and control over software supply chains. The goal of cloud sovereignty is therefore at risk of becoming a vehicle for policies that favor selected providers, restrict competition and fragment digital markets, ECIPE warns. Instead of allowing pan-European rivals for the big US cloud providers to grow and flourish, the framework may thus have the opposite effect in encouraging member states to favor providers within their own borders, leading to fragmentation across Europe. A more coherent approach would keep the resilience objectives, but temper their use through technological neutrality requirements that preserve interoperability, portability, and multi-cloud options, the report authors state. It makes a number of policy recommendations, including defining sovereignty as a demonstrated outcome, not an ownership status. “Real sovereignty means a public buyer can show its data is secure and that it can switch provider if it has to. A provider’s passport does not tell you that”, said ECIPE Director and co-author of the study, Fredrik Erixon. “Europe’s cloud market is already national in practice. CADA risks locking that in.” Vague drafting But not everyone might agree. Earlier this year, tech trade association CISPE (Cloud Infrastructure Service Providers in Europe) urged the European Commission to legislate for real tech sovereignty, rather than the illusion of it. It argued that sovereignty must be defined by control, not by whether a provider merely has an EU presence, and that means effective ownership of the underlying technology and protection from extraterritorial laws like the US CLOUD Act, under which Washington can compel American tech companies such as the big cloud operators, to hand over any data they hold, including data stored overseas. The same group had earlier warned that the EC’s criteria for cloud sovereignty had been drafted so vaguely as to favor incumbents – meaning the big American operators that already dominate Europe's cloud market. ®

item.title: Houdini act in Venice leaves Massimiliano Allegri searching for an escape at Napoli | Nicky Bandini
item.description: Manager’s latest setback exposed growing doubts about his squad and his approach as Davide Nicola began his Venezia tenure with a remarkable win “I’ll love you even if you win,” promised the Venezia supporter’s banner. More gallows humour from a fanbase that proved long ago that its relationship with the club could survive a defeat. They had endured six already in the first six rounds of this Serie A season: the only team in the division without a win or even a single point. The last time they were in Serie A, in 2024-25, Venezia finished 19th. The time before that, in 2021-22, they finished bottom. Deja vu all over again? item.title: Red Hat helps teach about tech writing
item.description: In Brno in Czechia, Red Hat’s large local office has been helping the city’s Masaryk University to teach future technical writers. Whenever someone tries to teach, though, they learn as well. At the Open Source Summit in Prague, a senior member of Red Hat’s documentation team in Brno presented a talk called Diagrams & Dragons: Teaching Technical Writing to University Students the Open Source Way . Red Hat has a large site in Brno, which is the second-largest Czech city and is also the home of the respected Masaryk University . Red Hat’s Brno office has a substantial documentation team — this vulture was part of it for a while. For the last four years, Red Hat has been working with the university’s Faculty of Informatics to teach a course unit in technical writing. Jiří Herrman talked about what the course tutors had learned from the students. For FI MUNI, its course PV177 Technical Writing. Red Hat has a page with some of the materials . “RH has been looking into cultivating technical writers in Brno for a while,” he said, but the launch of the course was “delayed due to the 2020 worldwide global… thingy.” The company particularly wants to work on what he described as “that tricky part of technical writing where you actually have to interact with other humans.” Some of the things that struck this former tech-docs writer the most are covered on pages 7 and 9 from Herrman’s short slide deck [PDF], which discuss what didn’t work. Although the course was aimed at students with some technical knowledge, they found that setting classwork with shell-based tools didn’t work: some of the students had never used the command-line, some came with borrowed laptops without admin-level access, and some came with just phones rather than laptops. item.dc:creator: Liam Proven
item.content:encoded: In Brno in Czechia, Red Hat’s large local office has been helping the city’s Masaryk University to teach future technical writers. Whenever someone tries to teach, though, they learn as well. At the Open Source Summit in Prague, a senior member of Red Hat’s documentation team in Brno presented a talk called Diagrams & Dragons: Teaching Technical Writing to University Students the Open Source Way . Red Hat has a large site in Brno, which is the second-largest Czech city and is also the home of the respected Masaryk University . Red Hat’s Brno office has a substantial documentation team — this vulture was part of it for a while. For the last four years, Red Hat has been working with the university’s Faculty of Informatics to teach a course unit in technical writing. Jiří Herrman talked about what the course tutors had learned from the students. For FI MUNI, its course PV177 Technical Writing. Red Hat has a page with some of the materials . “RH has been looking into cultivating technical writers in Brno for a while,” he said, but the launch of the course was “delayed due to the 2020 worldwide global… thingy.” The company particularly wants to work on what he described as “that tricky part of technical writing where you actually have to interact with other humans.” Some of the things that struck this former tech-docs writer the most are covered on pages 7 and 9 from Herrman’s short slide deck [PDF], which discuss what didn’t work. Although the course was aimed at students with some technical knowledge, they found that setting classwork with shell-based tools didn’t work: some of the students had never used the command-line, some came with borrowed laptops without admin-level access, and some came with just phones rather than laptops. Some we found less surprising. Getting students to grade one anothers’ work, much as professional tech writers review one another’s contributions, didn’t work well – partly due to the speed required. In the end, the compromise was to give the students a course in grading each other’s work “without pissing each other off.” It didn’t shock us, but we suspect might leave some training vendors taken aback, that interacting with remote teachers who were presenting online didn’t work well – especially when there were multiple tutors, changing with each class. LLM use You may well have already foreseen the biggest “gotcha” for a course that ran for the first time in 2023. It is, naturally, use of LLM. The students were told that they were not allowed to use LLMs during the course, but naturally enough, they did so anyway. Among the problems that Herrman reported were that giving praise to good work that involved LLM use just encouraged more cheating. However, telling students off for it discouraged them, and that encourages cheating. So the team had to come up with some tactics to try to manage this, which involved teaching the students how to use LLMs instead. They did, however, find some things that did work well. Awarding points, even on a semi-arbitrary basis, with occasional secret prizes, as well dispensing feedback via internet-style memes. A final exercise was to role-play a scenario, “Dungeons & Dragons” style. The quest was “I want to be a tech writer, but how to get there?”. This involved navigating a cross-functional team, creating things like release notes, technical notes, and some real documentation for the process. And as the course materials are open source, the graduates ended up with a permanent FOSS record that they can show to prospective employers. There is a project Github , and you can see some of the student’s archived coursework for 2025 and 2026 . The issues around LLM use in tech writing were the primary subject of a “Birds of a Feather” session that Herrman moderated earlier: Technical Writing in the Age of AI . He started by asking how many in the audience were using AI in their tech-writing efforts, getting what he called an “overwhelming majority” who were already on-board. What we found interesting is what people said they didn’t use it for. They find even the best models are poor at writing documentation themselves. They’re also poor at drawing diagrams, and at reading them for review purposes. They’re poor at reviewing docs (“AI is too obsequious and so reviews are overly positive,” and “it doesn’t give good feedback on user focus, or structure.”) However, most of the attendees found uses for it all the same. Examples included “Change management” and “Updating to new code” – in other words, identifying which parts of large products had changed and which therefore needed fresh documentation. Others said they used it for “Documenting decisions from meeting notes,” and in other ways, “Collecting information resources for writing,” and worryingly, to “Summarize notes (from conferences, meetings, etc.) and cluster by themes”. Another use was “Reverse engineering code to figure out intent,” or to “Find existing docs to prevent reinvention or duplication.” Tech writing is a demanding job, and pretty much permanently under-resourced. We can’t and don’t blame anyone for grabbing onto anything that might help. Even so, for us, what stood out from this session was the pretty much unanimous agreement among an audience of tech writers that LLMs were poor at doing the job that tech writers themselves did. Reviewing each others’ docs is a core part of the job: tech writers are used to this, and when they review the bots’ efforts, they find the machinese lacking. That fits our impressions, too. What we found alarming is that, although they find the bots poor at doing what the writers know best, even so, they trusted the bots to be competent in other functions, things the writers don’t look at so closely – for example, finding and selecting where docs need updating. The use for summarization is especially alarming: this is something that studies have demonstrated LLMs are bad at . They shorten, not summarize, and that’s no substitute. We find that worrying, but we regularly hear reports of companies pressing staff to use AI more. This is an all-too-human response: “it can’t do my job, but if I must use it, then this stuff isn’t my jurisdiction, and if it messes up, I can blame someone else.” We just worry at whose desk this buck will eventually stop. ®

item.title: 'They're kind of goth': NASA spacecraft gives mysterious brown dwarfs a close-up
item.description: null Using NASA’s SPHEREx spacecraft, astronomers have studied a host of "failed stars," also known as brown dwarfs. These strange cosmic bodies straddle the line between planets and stars, possessing a mass between 13 and 80 times that of Jupiter (0.013 to 0.08 times the mass of the sun ). They get the nickname failed stars because they form like stars from collapsing clouds of gas and dust but fail to gather enough mass to trigger the fusion of hydrogen to helium in their cores, the process that powers actual stars . This formation process also means that brown dwarfs are cosmic loners, wandering the darkness of space alone, bereft of the light of a parent star. That description might sound like lyrics from a Type O Negative song ("Black No. 1," anybody?). And that's apt, according to the leader of the new study, which reveals that, chemically speaking, the atmospheres of these dark and cloudy worlds are not unlike those of our solar system's gas giant planets. "They’re kind of goth," Zafar Rustamkulov, of the California Institute of Technology (Caltech), said in a statement . "Unlike exoplanets , free-floating brown dwarfs are completely independent celestial objects that will fade into eternity alone. We’re still learning how complex they are." Rustamkulov added that, from Earth orbit, SPHEREx — short for Spectro-Photometer for the History of the Universe, Epoch of Reionization, and Ices Explorer — sees wavelengths of light that are nigh-impossible to see with telescopes on the ground because water in Earth’s atmosphere absorbs them. That is important for bringing brown dwarfs into the light. "We are picking up light from the deep, red clouds of brown dwarfs all over the sky," he said. A forest (of brown dwarfs) Brown dwarfs have been somewhat mysterious since their discovery in the 1990s, due to the fact that the small amount of nuclear fusion that occurs within them causes them to emit no more than a faint glow. That means that our understanding of their makeup, their storms, and their evolution really only comes from theory. To help lift this observational darkness, the team turned to data from SPHEREx. They studied 37 nearby brown dwarfs in a spectrum of light including 102 wavelengths, from the deepest red our eyes can see to the invisible infrared light. These local failed stars spanned the full temperature range for brown dwarfs — from 4,000 degrees Fahrenheit to minus 10 degrees Fahrenheit (2,200 to minus 20 degrees Celsius). Considering that the temperature of the sun is about 10,000 degrees Fahrenheit (5,500 degrees Celsius), you could definitely say brown dwarfs run cold. Brown dwarfs observed by SPHEREx. (Image credit: Zafar Rustamkulov/NASA/JPL-Caltech) The spectra of brown dwarfs seen by SPHEREx allowed the team to determine that their atmospheres are chemically rich in water, carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide and methane. item.dc:creator: Robert Lea
item.content:encoded: null Using NASA’s SPHEREx spacecraft, astronomers have studied a host of "failed stars," also known as brown dwarfs. These strange cosmic bodies straddle the line between planets and stars, possessing a mass between 13 and 80 times that of Jupiter (0.013 to 0.08 times the mass of the sun ). They get the nickname failed stars because they form like stars from collapsing clouds of gas and dust but fail to gather enough mass to trigger the fusion of hydrogen to helium in their cores, the process that powers actual stars . This formation process also means that brown dwarfs are cosmic loners, wandering the darkness of space alone, bereft of the light of a parent star. That description might sound like lyrics from a Type O Negative song ("Black No. 1," anybody?). And that's apt, according to the leader of the new study, which reveals that, chemically speaking, the atmospheres of these dark and cloudy worlds are not unlike those of our solar system's gas giant planets. "They’re kind of goth," Zafar Rustamkulov, of the California Institute of Technology (Caltech), said in a statement . "Unlike exoplanets , free-floating brown dwarfs are completely independent celestial objects that will fade into eternity alone. We’re still learning how complex they are." Rustamkulov added that, from Earth orbit, SPHEREx — short for Spectro-Photometer for the History of the Universe, Epoch of Reionization, and Ices Explorer — sees wavelengths of light that are nigh-impossible to see with telescopes on the ground because water in Earth’s atmosphere absorbs them. That is important for bringing brown dwarfs into the light. "We are picking up light from the deep, red clouds of brown dwarfs all over the sky," he said. A forest (of brown dwarfs) Brown dwarfs have been somewhat mysterious since their discovery in the 1990s, due to the fact that the small amount of nuclear fusion that occurs within them causes them to emit no more than a faint glow. That means that our understanding of their makeup, their storms, and their evolution really only comes from theory. To help lift this observational darkness, the team turned to data from SPHEREx. They studied 37 nearby brown dwarfs in a spectrum of light including 102 wavelengths, from the deepest red our eyes can see to the invisible infrared light. These local failed stars spanned the full temperature range for brown dwarfs — from 4,000 degrees Fahrenheit to minus 10 degrees Fahrenheit (2,200 to minus 20 degrees Celsius). Considering that the temperature of the sun is about 10,000 degrees Fahrenheit (5,500 degrees Celsius), you could definitely say brown dwarfs run cold. Brown dwarfs observed by SPHEREx. (Image credit: Zafar Rustamkulov/NASA/JPL-Caltech) The spectra of brown dwarfs seen by SPHEREx allowed the team to determine that their atmospheres are chemically rich in water, carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide and methane. "We’re seeing the signatures of these molecules and how they change from object to object across the entire temperature regime," said team member J. Davy Kirkpatrick, also of Caltech. "Our paper concentrated on just three dozen, but we have thousands more that we are in the process of analyzing. "I really want to see what bounds the universe places on the variety of brown dwarfs." All my colors Brown dwarfs have been routinely observed by other telescopes, including NASA's James Webb Space Telescope and the agency's now-retired Spitzer Space Telescope , but the wide wavelength coverage of SPHEREx has made it particularly useful in observing these failed stars. That's good news for astronomers waiting for change in the atmospheres of brown dwarfs as they age and grow cold. The researchers found that some brown dwarfs observed by SPHEREx are at a stage of extreme change in which their clouds are clearing, creating atmospheres rich in methane. The team may have discovered significant new details about brown dwarfs, but they are still on the proverbial mystery street when it comes to these strange celestial objects, "The state-of-the-art models are capturing the general chemical trend, but when it comes to these cloudy transitions, the models are struggling to match the data," said Rustamkulov. "No two brown dwarfs are alike. Even at the same temperature, their spectra look quite distinct." NASA’s SPHEREx reveals molecules like methane (CH4), carbon dioxide (CO2), and carbon monoxide (CO) in brown dwarf atmospheres. The telescope’s view of three different brown dwarfs appears on the left. (Image credit: Zafar Rustamkulov/International Gemini Observatory/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA, M.H. Wong (UC Berkeley) et al. Acknowledgments: M. Zamani) "This journey has turned many of us into accidental meteorologists. We know how hard it is to predict weather on our own planet, and we realize it's going to be just as challenging to explain the phenomena we see in these bizarre, cold objects," Kirkpatrick said. "The findings are a call to action to explore even more of these dark worlds." As astronomers resond to that call to action, I will ponder how I could have worked Bauhaus' Goth classic "Bela Lugosi is Dead" into this article. The team's research was published on Sept. 28 in The Astrophysical Journal.

item.title: Brighton are the apex B club – their next target should be a Champions League place | Jonathan Wilson
item.description: Diego Gómez’s wondergoal in a five-star demolition is just the latest in an impressive run of results for the south coast team Sign up for our free newsletter here For two or three years now, it’s been standard to nod approvingly at how well-run Brighton, Brentford and Bournemouth are, and to move on. What else is there to say? It’s true, of course – these are sides who have made the most of relatively limited resources. But there’s also an underlying assumption in the designation: that these are clubs who have no higher aspiration, that their limit is earning praise for upper mid-table finishes. This season, perhaps, offers an opportunity to change that. Other than Arsenal, every major club is undergoing significant transition. Manchester City may have started the season with seven straight wins, but there’s every chance the punishment for their multiple breaches of Premier League regulations takes them out of the race for the top five. In that context, why shouldn’t one of those efficient smaller sides qualify for the Champions League? Continue reading...

item.title: Uber dodges £340M cabbie lawsuit after drivers miss legal deadline
item.description: Uber has dodged a £340 million lawsuit brought by thousands of London black cab drivers after a High Court judge ruled that they'd left it too late to sue. Monday's ruling kills off two claims involving around 13,000 cabbies and former private hire companies Kabbee and Iride, which accused Uber of misleading Transport for London (TfL) to secure its operating license. The cabbies wanted nearly £200 million in compensation for lost earnings, while Kabbee and Iride sought another £140 million. But the court never got as far as deciding whether Uber had done anything wrong. The claims were filed in May and June 2024, but Mr Justice Simon Birt ruled they were too late under the six-year time limit. The cabbies insisted that they hadn't had enough evidence to allege fraud until June 2018, but the judge wasn't buying it. According to the judgment, seen by The Register , three cabbies had already filed their own claims against Uber in September 2017. Litigation funder Harbour approached law firm Mishcon de Reya about a larger lawsuit that December, and by February 2018, the Licensed Taxi Drivers' Association was telling members about the planned action. The dispute dates back to Uber's arrival in London in 2012. The claimants alleged that the company deliberately misled TfL about how its booking system worked, allowing it to operate when it shouldn't have been permitted to do so. Uber has some history here. In a separate licensing appeal in 2018, the company admitted that it gave TfL and the High Court false information about how bookings were accepted through its app. The magistrate stopped short of finding dishonesty, however, and granted Uber a new 15-month license. The judgment also revisits Greyball, Uber's software for identifying suspected regulators, and Ripley, a tool used to remotely lock computers during regulatory visits. Uber maintained that Ripley hadn't been used that way in the UK. The cabbies insisted that they needed information from the June 2018 licensing appeal to support their fraud allegations. Justice Birt disagreed, finding that enough information had been available earlier to bring a claim. Things then went quiet. Mishcon sent Uber a letter before action in July 2019, but Harbour pulled its funding that November. The claimants didn't write to Uber again about the potential lawsuit for another four and a half years, according to the judgment, and by the time proceedings began in 2024, the deadline had passed. The ruling is a victory for Uber, but doesn't clear it of the alleged fraud. The judge dismissed the claims because they were filed too late, without deciding whether the allegations, which Uber denies, were true. Neither Uber nor RGL Management, the company representing the cabbies, responded to The Register ’s questions. London's taxi wars are far from over. item.title: ‘Leaving England is scary but I’m here to win’: Charlie Cresswell on Ligue 1 life and his international dream
item.description: Young centre-back could not see a way forward at Leeds so moved to France. Now he’s preparing for the biggest game of his life against Juventus By Get French Football News “Leaving England is such a scary, scary decision,” says Charlie Cresswell. It is a decision that he never thought he would make. His father, Richard, made a career as a footballer in England; his brother, Alfie, was coming through Leeds’ academy; Charlie was on the fringes of their first team when the opportunity arose to join Toulouse in 2024. “That was the biggest decision I made in football,” he says. “I’ve been a Leeds fan since I was eight. I’d been at the club since I was 10, but, looking back, I was 20 years old with no games and I needed to get out and go play.” Continue reading...

item.title: Olamide Ehinfun-Adekunle Becomes Nigeria’s Youngest Female Senior Advocate of Nigeria at 40
item.description: Judicial portrait of Olamide Mojigbotoluwa Ehinfun-Adekunle SAN, partner at Afe Babalola & Co., who made history as Nigeria’s youngest female Senior Advocate of Nigeria at the age of 40. Nigeria’s legal landscape has witnessed a momentous record as Olamide Mojigbotoluwa Ehinfun – Adekunle joins the prestigious Inner Bar, officially becoming the youngest female Senior Advocate of Nigeria (SAN) in history. Attaining the highly coveted Silk rank at the age of 40, the seasoned advocate and solicitor of the Supreme Court of Nigeria has broken a long-standing ceiling, setting a inspiring milestone for women across the legal profession and beyond. Olamide Mojigbotoluwa Ehinfun-Adekunle, MCIArb, is a distinguished partner at the renowned law firm Afe Babalola & Co. (Emmanuel Chambers). With a career spanning over 14 years of legal practice, she specialises in complex litigation, commercial dispute resolution, strategic legal advisory, and international arbitration. Olamide Ehinfun-Adekunle SAN following her elevation as the youngest female Senior Advocate of Nigeria. Her academic foundation includes a Bachelor of Laws (LL.B.) degree from Obafemi Awolowo University, Ile-Ife, and a Master of Laws (LL.M.) in International Trade Law from the University of Leeds, United Kingdom. Before joining Afe Babalola & Co. as a Partner in September 2013, her professional experience included key positions at D. D. Dodo & Co. and the Nuhu Ribadu Campaign Organisation. Her historic elevation to Senior Advocate of Nigeria—a position reserved for legal practitioners who have distinguished themselves through exceptional skill, professional integrity, and significant contributions to Nigerian jurisprudence—marks a defining moment in contemporary law. Taking on the rank at 40 years old, she stands out as the youngest female lawyer to achieve this honour in Nigeria, carving a clear path for future generations of female lawyers to aim for the highest levels of leadership in the country’s judiciary and private bar. Olamide Mojigbotoluwa Ehinfun-Adekunle, Nigeria’s youngest female Senior Advocate of Nigeria (SAN). Nigeria’s legal landscape has witnessed a momentous record as Olamide Mojigbotoluwa Ehinfun – Adekunle joins the prestigious Inner Bar, officially becoming the youngest female Senior Advocate of Nigeria (SAN) in history. Attaining the highly coveted Silk rank at the age of 40, the seasoned advocate and solicitor of the Supreme Court of Nigeria has broken a long-standing ceiling, setting a inspiring milestone for women across the legal profession and beyond. Olamide Mojigbotoluwa Ehinfun-Adekunle, MCIArb, is a distinguished partner at the renowned law firm Afe Babalola & Co. (Emmanuel Chambers). With a career spanning over 14 years of legal practice, she specialises in complex litigation, commercial dispute resolution, strategic legal advisory, and international arbitration. Olamide Ehinfun-Adekunle SAN following her elevation as the youngest female Senior Advocate of Nigeria. Her academic foundation includes a Bachelor of Laws (LL.B.) degree from Obafemi Awolowo University, Ile-Ife, and a Master of Laws (LL.M.) in International Trade Law from the University of Leeds, United Kingdom. Before joining Afe Babalola & Co. as a Partner in September 2013, her professional experience included key positions at D. D. Dodo & Co. and the Nuhu Ribadu Campaign Organisation. Her historic elevation to Senior Advocate of Nigeria—a position reserved for legal practitioners who have distinguished themselves through exceptional skill, professional integrity, and significant contributions to Nigerian jurisprudence—marks a defining moment in contemporary law. Taking on the rank at 40 years old, she stands out as the youngest female lawyer to achieve this honour in Nigeria, carving a clear path for future generations of female lawyers to aim for the highest levels of leadership in the country’s judiciary and private bar. Olamide Mojigbotoluwa Ehinfun-Adekunle, Nigeria’s youngest female Senior Advocate of Nigeria (SAN). item.title: Calls to strengthen workplace privacy in Australia as employers turn to AI to track staff
item.description: Monitoring tools common in a range of workplaces, including factories, office jobs, delivery work and in retail – often without employees being informed Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Employers are increasingly using technology, from CCTV to keystroke monitoring, to track workers’ moves and it is being accelerated by the use of AI, the Human Technology Institute has warned. Examples provided to Guardian Australia by the institute include a fast-food restaurant using surveillance cameras to stop workers using their phones, and AI tracking leading to a cashier warned over making a mistake once every 533 scans. Continue reading...
